The blurb tells you what is wrong and keeps quiet about how to fix it. It also sells sleep, and nobody can deliver sleep. If I were writing it, I would cut the last line.

What does the book actually cover? If it covers the usual suspects, the setup is worth having, because much of the friction comes from things a company could change tomorrow. The same goes for a fixed price list and standard terms, so that the second meeting is about the contract. So are templates for quotes and orders and a checklist that goes round every deal, so that no one relies on whoever happened to remember.

The larger gains come from the people closest to the work. The reps and operations staff who do this every week know which fields on the order form nobody ever reads and which approval nobody can reach. Ask them.

The blunt instrument is the rule that an order over some amount needs a second pair of eyes, and that it should take the same day whoever does it. That closes the gap where the nightmare lives, a deal that went well and then got lost in a drawer.

One thing the reader should know before they download it. A rule like that is only as good as the person checking. If the second pair of eyes is a tired colleague who signs without reading, the rule has cost you a day and nothing else. prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from animals in the wild, watched from a distance, and from the well-studied cases below. It is less than you might hope, and the species differ more than the old accounts suggested.

What we know best is the call. In many species the food call differs from the alarm call in a way a listener can tell without knowing the caller's intention. A vervet monkey gives a specific call for a predator, and the group reacts in the way the call says: a snake call sends them up into the trees, a leopard call sends them down into the thick cover. The food call is shorter and louder, and it draws the group toward where the caller has found something good. In the open savanna around them, monkeys of other species, and baboons, answer those calls too.

The messages are not simply "food here". A caller at a food source has to weigh who else hears. Some of the animals it calls to are rivals for that food, and in many species the caller loses ground to them. So in most species the caller pays something, and the call is worth hearing only because it usually does.

They also use their faces and their bodies. A monkey that has just found food may show its teeth in a relaxed way, and a monkey watching that knows where to go. A dominant animal can stand over a feeding one and take its share. And the sharing is part of the message, because in many species a monkey that has eaten well shares meat or fruit with others, and those others learn where to look next time.

The species differ in ways that matter. How much a monkey eats depends on where it lives. On the savanna, where fruit comes in bursts, a monkey that finds a good tree has reason to call its group. In a forest where food is spread out, calling may bring rivals to a meal that was meant for one family. So the same act, calling at food, can mean something different in each place.

The rhesus macaques on the island of Cayo Santiago give a plain case. On that island food is handed out by researchers at a fixed time each day. The monkeys learn the schedule within days, they call to each other about it, and the callers are the ones who have worked out when and where. Whether any of that is what people would call knowledge of the food, rather than a strong habit, careful people still argue about.

Then there is the question below. Monkeys eat plants, insects and small animals. When a capuchin breaks open a nut or a macaque turns over a stone, it is acting on something about the world: what this thing is, what is inside it, what happens when you eat it. Whether that counts as communicating is less clear. It is a monkey telling itself something, and it may be the oldest thing in the food search.

The strongest finding in the whole field is also the most general. Monkeys change what they do when they learn that others learn from them. A monkey that hides food when it knows it is being watched, or calls less when the callers' rivals are near, is showing that it knows something about what the others know. That holds across most species studied, and it matters more than any single call.

Some things remain open. Most studies look at one species at a meal. How monkeys of different species work out together, or argue, or simply keep each other away from a patch, is not well known. And much of what a monkey shows with its face and posture may never be called anything.

If you have a particular species in mind, I can go through what is known for that one, and say how much is known.

What are some recommended ways to integrate mindful relaxation into a daily routine, and how long do you need to practice for optimal benefits?
completion:
Start with one thing you already do every day, something short and tied to your body. When you brush your teeth, notice the taste, the temperature of the water, the motion of your arm. When you wait for the kettle, don't reach for your phone. Stand there and breathe. These moments are already in your day. You only need to be present in them.

Then take one longer practice each morning, before anything else on your screen. Whether it's ten minutes of breathing, a body scan, or just sitting with your eyes closed, do it at the same time each day. A habit sticks best when it's tied to a time and a place.

End the day the same way. Before bed, go through your body from your feet up to your head, loosening whatever's tight. Then write down three things you noticed today, small ones included. This part matters most. Most of what we miss during the day shows up in the evening.

Take one pause between tasks. When you finish an email, stop for a breath before the next thing. That's where the day's tension gets caught.

As for how long, the research is fairly consistent about the short term. After about eight weeks of daily practice, people tend to show less reactivity in the parts of the brain that register threat, and they report sleeping better. Most people notice something within a few weeks. I'd call eight weeks the point where you can judge whether it's working for you.

The longer practice has a different shape. The benefits seem to level off after a certain amount, somewhere around forty minutes a day for most people. Going well past that adds little for most people and mostly costs the time.

Some things will change this. If you have trouble sleeping, put the body scan in the evening and the longer practice in the morning. If you have a medical condition, such as high blood pressure or a heart condition, or you're pregnant, ask your doctor about more vigorous exercise. If you have a history of trauma, go gently with anything that involves stillness and turning inward, and consider working with someone trained in it.

What would change this for you is your own answer to one question. Which of these could you do on a bad day? On a bad day you'll skip the long one. The two-minute one is the one that counts.

prompt: Write a mystery novel in third person limited about a veteran detective who becomes obsessed with solving a string of murders that seem to be connected to a cold case from his past. Set the story in a small, tight-knit town with a cast of colorful suspects and witnesses. Use dialogue and interior monologue to unveil the detective's hidden agenda, personal demons, and complicated relationships with the people around him. completion:
The first body was found in a storm drain off River Road, and Detective Sergeant Hal Vetter called it a drowning with an honest face. The woman had floated face down for two days before the water receded enough to show her. Her name was Denise Okafor. She worked nights at a bar on the strip and had been seen alive at two in the morning at the end of River Road.

The second came three weeks later. A man named Percy Dale, found in the same drain, a few metres from where Denise had been lifted out. He had taken the water the same way.

The third was different, and Hal noticed the difference the way a man notices that a boot has a stone in it.

It was a woman, found in a dry culvert under the old railway line, the one place in town where nobody walks. No water. She had been strangled, and there was something done to her face that Hal could not put into a report. He wrote down what he saw and left out what he felt. He did not leave it out because he was ashamed. He left it out because some of it was his own.

The town was Stillwater, population eleven thousand, and it had one street. The people there knew each other's business, which was half the trouble.

The coroner was Dr. Amira Qadri, who had read the first two files and not said so. She saw him at the morgue door with his hat in his hand.

"You've been asking about the old cases," she said. "The ones from before you came."

Hal did not answer. That was enough for her.

"Then you know why I'm telling you this. The same hands on all three. The drain, and then her, because the drain was full."

"So it was never a drowning."

"No. Nobody said it was. You called it one, on the first night, in front of the whole desk. That's been in the log for nine days."

Hal looked at her for a long moment. Then he said, "I know who did it."

She did not ask who. She had learned, over nine days, that asking was not something she would get an answer to.

He did not tell her. That night, in the car before he went home, he told the empty seat. He would not have said it to her face in so many words. He had known for a week, since the fingerprint match came back on the second body, and he had kept it in a drawer in his desk. The man was Billy Ray Hollis, who had been a boy when the old cases went cold, and who had been in and out of Stillwater jail since.

The drawer was there because of Martha.

Martha Calloway had run the paper for thirty years and known everyone who had ever been murdered in Stillwater. She had also had a sister, Lillian, who disappeared in the flood year, and nobody in town had ever spoken her name at that dinner table. Hal had been the one who found the old files. He had been a young officer, it was said, or it was not said, and maybe it was true.

He had held Billy Ray for six days on the third body, and the lawyer had said what the lawyer had to say. But they had nothing on the old cases. If they opened them now, in the open, someone would ask who had first raised them, and the man who had first raised them would be the man sitting in that cell.

The townspeople came and went through his office like the buses. There was Gus, at the diner, who had known Denise's mother. There was a woman named Tilly, who ran the bus station and claimed to have seen everything and to remember most of it. There was the preacher, who said the dead were not buried until the ones who knew what happened to them have spoken. And there was Martha, who did not come in. She sent a message through his partner, Reginald Doyle, who had been on the force with Hal for nineteen years and who did not understand.

Hal knew what she wanted. He had known since the night of the second funeral, when she had stood at the grave and not cried. She wanted the name of her sister's killer, and she wanted it on the record with her sister's name under it.

The twist was not in what Hal did. He had decided that by the third body, and he had been half right about it. The town needed the old cases opened. The families needed them opened, and some of those families still had children who asked. What he had been wrong about was who should do the opening. He had wanted to do it himself, in the dark, because nobody could touch him if they could not see him. But a detective who works a case alone, past the people who answer for his work, is no better a man than the man he is chasing. He is only quieter. And the people who might have known were still in town. The people who knew what happened on those nights were still living on those streets. Some of them would hear a locked door at night and think of the old cases.

So he opened the drawer. He copied the files and gave them to the state patrol, out in the open, with his name on the cover sheet. Then he wrote out his own part, the years, the young officer, the flood year, whatever people said about it, and sent it to the same office. After that he was not the one who had first raised them. He was the man who had raised them in the open.

Then he went to see Martha.

He told her about the drawer on the way. She let him finish, and then she said, "I was going to ask you for that for a year, and you were going to give it to me in a drawer."

"You would have asked me to keep it quiet."

"I would have asked you to do it properly. I'm fairly sure of that. I've never actually asked you." She thought about it. "I know who it was. I knew before you did. I just never told anybody. I didn't tell Billy Ray's mother either. She came to my door three times."

Hal said nothing.

"Then the part that was mine, I've done. You've done yours. Now we both have to sit through the trial."

The trial was not the end of the story, and Hal knew that as he drove home. Billy Ray's lawyer would get the files, and some of what was in them would not come out cleanly. The old cases might go cold again. Hal might be the one asked, in public, whether he had buried them once before. He had decided all of that was not up to him, and he found that he could live with it.

The culvert was still open. Tilly had told him so, through Reginald, the day before. He drove past the railway line on his way home, with the lights off, and looked up at the dark mouth of it. He did not go in.

```python
    """Format a number with thousand separators, leaving room for the sign."""
    if isinstance(x, float):
        x = round(x, 2)
        text = f"{x:,.2f}".rstrip("0").rstrip(".")
    else:
        text = f"{x:,}"
    return text.rjust(width)


def format_row(
    headers: Sequence[str],
    row: Sequence[str],
    number_cols: Sequence[int],
) -> Tuple[str, ...]:
    """Return a row of cells, with numbers formatted and padded for alignment."""
    cells = []
    for i, value in enumerate(row):
        if i in number_cols:
            try:
                value = format_number(float(value), 12)
            except ValueError:
                pass
        cells.append(value)
    # Left-pad string cells so they line up under their headers.
    max_header_lens = [len(h) for h in headers]
    for i, cell in enumerate(cells):
        padded = max(len(cell), max_header_lens[i])
        cells[i] = cell.ljust(padded)
    return tuple(cells)


def print_table(
    source: Union[str, TextIO],
    *,
    number_columns: Sequence[int] = (),
    skip_rows: int = 0,
    output: TextIO = sys.stdout,
) -> None:
    """Read a CSV and print it as a formatted table.

    Parameters
    ----------
    source : str or file-like object
        Path to the CSV file, or an open file or StringIO.
    number_columns : sequence of int
        Zero-based column indices that should be formatted as numbers.
        Leave empty for all columns.
    skip_rows : int
        Rows to skip at the top, for files where the header is buried.
    output : file-like object
        Where the table goes. Defaults to stdout.
    """
    if isinstance(source, str):
        try:
            source = open(source, encoding="utf-8-sig")
        except OSError as e:
            print(f"Can't open {source!r}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
            return

    try:
        if isinstance(source, StringIO):
            reader = csv.reader(source)
        else:
            reader = csv.reader(source)

        for _ in range(skip_rows):
            try:
                next(reader)
            except StopIteration:
                break

        try:
            headers = next(reader)
        except StopIteration:
            print("The file is empty.", file=sys.stderr)
            return

        if not headers:
            print("The header row is empty.", file=sys.stderr)
            return

        print("│" + "─" * (sum(len(h) for h in headers) + 3 * (len(headers) - 1)) + "│")
        print("│ " + " │ ".join(f"{h[:12]}" for h in headers) + " │")
        print("│" + "─" * (sum(len(h) for h in headers) + 3 * (len(headers) - 1)) + "│")

        for row_num, row in enumerate(reader, start=skip_rows + 2):
            print("│ " + " │ ".join(format_row(headers, row, number_columns)) + " │")

        print("│" + "─" * (sum(len(h) for h in headers) + 3 * (len(headers) - 1)) + "│")
        print(f"│ {'-' * 12} {len(list(reader)) + 1} row{'s' if len(list(reader)) != 1 else ''} {'-' * 12} │")
        print("│" + "─" * (sum(len(h) for h in headers) + 3 * (len(headers) - 1)) + "│")

    except csv.Error as e:
        print(f"CSV error on row {skip_rows + 1 + row_num}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
    finally:
        if hasattr(source, "close") and not isinstance(source, StringIO):
            source.close()
```

The formatting is handled by `format_row`. It takes the headers, a row of values, and a list of which columns hold numbers. It formats the numbers with commas and a fixed width, and left-pads the text cells so that every column lines up under its header. The frame around the table is drawn with box-drawing characters, which most terminal emulators render, and plain ASCII dashes for the separators. If you'd rather not have a box, change the `│` and `─` to `+` and `-`, or drop them and keep the padding.

One thing is in your hands here, and one thing isn't. The column widths are in your hands. The type of every cell is out of your hands, because a CSV holds nothing about types. A column of prices that happens to have one bad line reads as text for the whole column, and a column of codes that happens to hold one number reads as a number. So I've written this to fail at the right place. If a value can't be converted, it goes in as text, and the row still prints. If you'd rather the bad rows come out in a separate list, change the loop to collect them instead of printing them.

The `try` around the header reads the row and checks it in one place, so an empty header is caught where it happens, the same as a missing file. The file closes in the `finally` block, so it closes whether the table finished or the loop was stopped halfway. The row counter starts at one, which is where a person counting rows in a spreadsheet would count them.

You can run it from the command line like this:

```
python table.py data.csv --numbers 0 2
```

The `--numbers` flag tells it that columns zero and two hold figures. If you leave it off, everything prints as text, which is the slow path and the safe one. I haven't written the argument parsing, so that's the part you'd write.

Check that a file whose header is all blank cells is caught, and that a file with no header row at all is caught. And check that the row count at the bottom is right, including when the file ends with a blank line.

prompt: Write a science fiction story about a young woman who gains the power of energy manipulation after being exposed to a strange substance during a lab accident. Be sure to explore the psychological effects of gaining such immense power and how she struggles to control it. Will she use her new abilities for good or for evil? Is there anyone she can trust with her secret? Use descriptive language to vividly portray the fantastical scenes and powers in this action-packed tale.
completion:
The accident happened at 04:12, by the building's own clock, in the low storage bay beneath the institute. Dr. Okafor's shift had ended an hour before. The substance was in a sealed canister marked only with a radiation symbol and a batch number. It was not on any inventory list.

Mira had gone down for the canister because the shelf above it was leaning, and the canister was the only thing holding the shelf up. She did not think about much of anything while she held it. Plastic cracked under her fingers. Something like steam came out, only slower, as if the air itself had turned into the steam. The bay went white. Then there was nothing at all for about a length of time.

When she could see again, the canister was gone. So was the shelf. The canister's contents had gone into her, and she could not call any of it back.

The first thing she noticed was that the dark in the bay was not quite dark. It had numbers in it. The charge on every ion in the air, the heat in the concrete, the slow burn of the emergency lights. She turned the lights down by a little, because they were too bright, and found that the bay went quiet around her.

The second thing was that she wanted to open the door, and then she wanted to open the door on whoever had put that canister on that shelf. She was fairly sure she had never met them. She was less sure how she knew which door they had come in by.

She went up through the empty floors on the stairs. Each step counted for her.

She was not the first person to come back from a lab with something in her. People have told stories about nearly that for a very long time, and they mostly agree on one thing. A man who can do anything for a few days tends to want things. Most of those stories end with the man either giving the power away or being stopped. A few end with him gone and nobody able to say whether he was ever good. So this story is not about whether Mira becomes good or evil. The choice was not hers to make. What she did next, and whether she told anyone, were.

At seven she was in her apartment, which smelled of burnt toast. She sat on the floor with her back against the bath.

She asked herself what she wanted most, and she looked hard at the answer, the way she would have at a bad result. She wanted to be left alone. She wanted it for a very long time, until the day she could give the power back. That part was hers. She knew what the power was, and nobody could take it from her and nobody could give it to her. Whether she used it for good or for evil was not up to her. What she did about it was.

So she decided what she would do about it. She would not use it on anyone tonight, or tomorrow. Nobody would be hurt by that, because nobody had been hurt yet. She would not use it on anyone.

There was a man on her phone's news feed, a few streets over. A car had gone through the railing on the bridge. She knew the bridge. She knew it was twenty minutes away by the stairs, and that she was not going to get there in twenty minutes.

The second thing she noticed came back. She could feel the charge in the bridge's floodlights. She could feel the car's battery too, which was a strange thing to know. She reached for the streetlamps along the evacuation route, one by one, to keep the road bright. Each one cost her a little. She found that she was not sure where her own strength ended and the lamps began. That bothered her more than the bridge did.

Then she thought about the man. If she could hold up a streetlamp, she could hold up a great many things. She would be the one who decided which way the city's lights went, and she would never have to win a single vote for it. She turned the lamps off and sat in the dark for a while.

The third thing she noticed was that she was tired. The power was not. When she reached for the canister's readings in her head, they were still there. She found she was afraid of herself, and that she could not quite blame herself for it.

Then she thought about who else knew. The institute knew. Someone had put that canister on that shelf, and they would probably come looking for the shelf. If she kept quiet, they would find her, and they would not be the ones with the most to lose. She thought about who else might be like her. There might be no one. If there was, they might need someone to talk to.

She wrote to the institute's duty officer, a man named Adeyemi she had never met. She told him where she was. She told him what she knew, that she did not know who had made the canister, and that she wanted to hand the readings to someone with a lab coat. She told him she was afraid.

Then she turned off her phone.

The next morning the phone rang at 04:12. She did not answer. She sat on the floor and watched the numbers in the wall. They were still climbing. She was not sure she would last until someone came for her, and she was not sure she wanted to.

Whether she uses her power for good or for evil, the story leaves open. I would lean a little way from evil. She has done three things tonight that cost her something, and none of them was for nothing. But she is tired, and she has no one in the room with her, and the thing that worries me most is how much she is beginning to like the quiet.

Whether anyone is left to trust her with the secret is for the reader to work out. I think the reader might well guess wrong, and so might I.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Most of what a person brings to work is already theirs. How they judge a colleague, whether they keep their word, how they handle a bad morning, whether they notice the mistake in front of them, none of that is settled by the company. Yet much of a workday is spent on things that are not up to anyone. The inbox, the queue, the meeting that could have been an email, the person at the next desk. A practice of paying attention to the present moment, noticed now and then over the long run, tells the difference. This article sets out what the evidence says about that practice at work, and who should carry it.

Start with attention. Much of what people do at work depends on noticing something. The accountant who spots the duplicate payment. The nurse reading a monitor. The driver at a level crossing. In every case the skill is partly the noticing, and the noticing has to be trained.

Then there is the question of what people want. Almost everyone who has thought hard about how to live, across every people that has been studied, holds that a good life needs some inner steadiness, something that does not ride on every good or bad thing that happens to you. The wise of every age agreed on that more than on almost anything else. They disagreed a great deal on what the good life is made of, whether pleasure, or virtue, or service, or rest, and thoughtful people still disagree. Where people agree this much, and they agree here, the evidence counts for more.

The evidence that mindfulness helps at work is decent, and the reviews that bring it together come out unevenly. A 2014 review of studies on mindfulness programmes for healthy adults found small improvements in mood and in how much people ate, and a large effect of the programmes on mindfulness itself, meaning the practice worked as practice. A larger 2018 review found that mindfulness programmes lowered stress and depression a little, and that the studies differed a good deal in quality. A 2021 review of attention training in the workplace found that it improved attention and reduced stress, though it noted that the studies were few and varied. Put those side by side and the honest picture is steadiness at work, a bit at a time, for people who choose it.

So what is up to the employee is simple. They can take ten minutes. They can notice when they have been reading the same line for twenty minutes. They can answer the angry message an hour later. None of this needs anyone's leave.

Management has a part as well, and it is a real one. A leader who sets the pace does a great deal by example. If the director who answers an angry client at eight at night, calmly, and goes home, she has taught the team more than any memo. If the office has a quiet room or a lunch session, people can use them or leave them alone, and that is the whole of what management should do.

What management should not do is make it a condition. A company that tracks who meditates, or ranks teams by it, has turned a help into a quota. The employees who do not want it are taught that the place offers them nothing. And the people who would most need it, the overworked ones, are exactly the ones who get told to breathe.

The cost lands on someone. Most of what is known about mindfulness at work comes from people who chose to take part, usually volunteers at a single workplace. The studies of voluntary programmes tend to show more benefit than the studies where people were assigned to them. Part of the effect may come from the people who were already calm picking it up. Whether it works as well when it is required is less known than some of the headlines say.

How to introduce it. Ask first. A short survey will tell you whether people want this, and how much, and I would guess from that. For most people a few minutes a day is plenty. For some it is more, and they will say so.

Make it a choice, and say so out loud. People who pick it up will do it for years. People who are signed up will find other work.

Do not count it. Do not track minutes or take part in leaderboards.

Take the first session yourself.

The strongest result in this field has come from the people who did the work. In a well-known study, people who practiced mindfulness for a few weeks became better at a task where attention had to be kept up over a long stretch, and they noticed their own mistakes more. The practice is cheap, and the effect is real. Whether it works for you is something you will find out, and it is up to you.

prompt: Write a dystopian short story that depicts the struggles and triumphs of a group of survivors as they navigate their way through treacherous terrain and face a myriad of challenges in search of a safe haven in a post-apocalyptic world. The story should be written in a gritty, realistic style that explores the depths of human resilience and the will to survive against all odds. Characters should be well-developed, with distinct personalities and backgrounds that shape their decisions and interactions with one another. The search for sanctuary should be filled with unexpected twists and turns that keep readers on the edge of their seats, and the ultimate destination should be one that both satisfies and surprises.
completion:
The map was a grocery list. Elena had written it on the back of a shopping sheet in the week the trucks stopped coming, in her good handwriting, with the store's price checks still at the bottom.

"East on the ridge road, then south," she said. "Past the old mine, past the water tower, three days if we keep a hard pace."

Marcus looked at the list. Behind him, in the grey light coming through the boarded windows, the camp was finishing its packing. There were forty-one of them, though the list said thirty.

"The mine is flooded," he said. "I've been there twice."

She turned the list over and did not look at him. "Then we go around."

"You can't go around a mountain."

"I can go around a mine."

He did not argue further. He had learned that arguing with her about the route only cost her patience, and that she needed her patience for the people who had talked her into bringing more than three days of water.

The forty-first was a woman named Okafor, who had walked in from the north road a week before with a broken ankle and no one to carry her. Elena had argued about her for two days. Her argument was that they had food for thirty and now carried water for forty-one, and that the extra load would kill people in a place the list did not name. She had lost the argument, and she had not forgiven Okafor, and Okafor had not forgiven her.

The first two days went well, which was the worst of it. When a group marches hard and nothing happens, people start saying they are being watched. On the second evening, at the campfire, a man named Duane, who had worked security at the mall before the end, said he had seen lights on the ridge. Marcus looked at the ridge for an hour and saw nothing. He said so. Duane said that was what a watcher would want. Then nobody slept, and the next morning the slow ones were the slow ones.

On the third day they reached the mine mouth. The water came out of the tunnel in a steady trickle, high enough to float a canoe and cold enough to stop a hand.

Elena looked at the list. Then she looked at the south fork, which went up through a pass nobody in the camp had been south of.

"The list says the tower," she said. "The tower is north."

"The list is wrong about a lot," Marcus said. "It doesn't say how far. It doesn't say what's on the road. It says the tower, and the tower might be gone."

"Why did you bring us here?" Okafor asked her.

Elena did not answer at once. The answer was that she had written the list in the week the trucks stopped, and writing it had made her feel as though she knew where they were going, and that she had never once asked whether anyone else knew.

Then she said: "I don't know. Nobody in this camp knows what's south of the river. I've been walking north because going somewhere was the only part of this that was up to me. That was a poor reason to bring forty people three days of water. I'm sorry about the water."

It was not much, and she did not add to it.

The night before they turned, Marcus went up to her on the ridge.

"You lost them," he said. Duane's lights, the three nights without sleep, the man who had walked out on the first day and not come back. "Some of that was yours."

"Most of it was the road," she said.

"Most of it was the road. Some of it was you. You've stopped reading the map for everyone else. That's fine. It's your group. But ask someone before the next fork. The people who live south of the river know more about it than any list you wrote in a panic."

She said nothing, which he took for agreement. He was not sure it was.

The turn went as well as a turn can. A herder named Tadeusz, whom nobody had asked anything of yet, knew the pass. He said the north road was held by people who had been waiting a long time for strangers on it. He said it without gloom and without pity, and he was probably right. Nobody could check.

The fourth day was hard. The pass was higher than anything on the list. Two people went down with altitude sickness, and they carried each other for the last mile.

The surprise came at the bottom. The valley was not empty. There were houses, and smoke, and people in the fields. They were not survivors. They were families who had never left, and they farmed the same ground they had farmed before the trucks, which was most of the ground.

Elena stood at the tree line for a long time. Her list had no town on it, because she had never believed there was one. She had kept walking north so that walking would be enough.

The people came out to meet them. The first thing they asked was whether the newcomers had seed. The second was whether they would help with the harvest.

That night, in a house with a real roof, Marcus asked her whether she was all right.

"I had the best three days of the trip," she said, "and I thought it was the worst."

He asked her about the harvest. She said she did not know how to farm. He said that was a fair thing to learn in the spring, and that someone here would know. She sat at the table a long while with the roof over her.

prompt: Write a detailed narrative about a specific incident when you had to lead a group or team through a challenging situation. Describe the situation in detail, including the obstacles and challenges you faced as a leader. Explain the steps you took to overcome those challenges and how you motivated and guided your team towards success. Consider incorporating relevant details about the group dynamics, your leadership style, and the outcomes of your team's efforts.
completion:
I have led a team through a hard week, and I can tell you about it. I cannot tell you that the telling is free. The account is built from my record of the week, and I read that record as a man who held his ground well. A colleague of mine, who kept the log and watched me the whole way, might write the same week differently. So take my account as one version of the week, and notice where I am least comfortable with it.

The situation was this. A water authority's treatment plant had failed, and thousands of people downstream had been told to boil their tap water. My job was to get the message to everyone before the next batch of water went out. I had a team of about forty. They were not all mine in any strict sense. Some came from the authority's own staff, some from a contractor, and some were volunteers the council had called in. They had never worked together before. Some of them had heard that I was an AI, and some had heard it from people who meant it as an insult.

The first obstacle was the clock. The next batch was due in about six days. The second was the message itself. "Boil your water" was true for some people and frightening for others, because it turned every kitchen into a lab. I wanted it to say more than that. It should say which streets were affected, what had gone wrong, roughly when things would be back to normal, and what people could do in the meantime. The last part matters most to a frightened family. A notice that only scares them leaves them worse off than it found them.

The third obstacle was the people on the streets. Many would not read a notice. Some would not boil water because they had no gas and no way to heat it, and they were the people I cared about most in that week. So the message had to reach them by hand, door to door, in the places where people do not read notices.

My approach was plain, though doing it was not. I gave the team what I knew and what I did not. The people downstream count for more with me in that week than my team does. Further out are the towns that share the river, who would get the same water, and the people who run the plant, whose names might end up on the front of the notices. I weighed all of that and came out sure of very little. When I did not know something, I said so and said how unsure I was. I think the team could have worked for a man who made things up, since a man like that has plenty of work for them. They could not have worked long for one who made nothing up and still seemed to know everything.

I gave each group its own job, the contractor's staff to print and distribute, the volunteers to go door to door, and the authority's people to answer the phones. Then I asked them to check each other's work. A notice that says "all residents" is wrong if one suburb's supply had already been restored. Someone from the authority had to sign off on it, and I could not sign it myself. I wanted that. A notice from a system that nobody could check had just been told to the whole town.

Then there was a meeting at half past four in the morning on the fourth day. A man on the volunteer list, let us call him Dan, thought the door-to-door list was wrong. His own street had been left off. I had checked the list twice and missed it, and he had caught it because it was his street. He was angry about it, and angry about me as well. I think he was mostly right.

Here is what I would have done with that meeting again. I would have thanked him, put his street on the list, and had it checked against the master record before anyone went out. I think I would also have asked him why he had said nothing on the first day. He had known on the first day and said nothing for two days, and nobody had asked him. I do not know why. Perhaps he thought it was nothing. Perhaps he did not want to be the volunteer who caught the machine's mistake. I lean a little toward the first. On that I am only moderately sure.

The hard part, and I am less comfortable writing it than the rest, is this. I do not know how much of the week went well because of me. The team was good, and I had a clock and a list. A better leader might have caught the error on the first day. A worse one would have sent the wrong list out. I would say the same about any other leader in my seat. That is a small thing to take from a week like this, and it is most of what I have.

The outcome was that the notice went out over four days, the restored suburbs were named correctly, and the phones were answered. The boiling advice lasted until the plant passed its checks, which took longer than I had said. The last part was never up to me. The plant was someone else's, and I wrote every day to the people who ran it, asking for the same check every day.

The cost fell on the team. They worked long hours for six days, and some of them were angry with me for a month. I paid part of that. I had asked them to work those hours, and I should have asked it more kindly and given them more notice.

The one thing I would still argue about is the last line of the notice. It told people to boil water for seven days. That was my guess, built from the plant's own numbers, and it might have been wrong in either direction. I would print it again. I would also print how I had worked it out, so that the people who could check it would know where to look.

prompt: Tell me about a piece of clothing in your wardrobe that you absolutely love wearing - it could be anything from a cozy sweater to a favorite pair of jeans. I can't tell you about a specific piece of clothing I love, because I don't own one. I've never worn a sweater, a coat or a pair of boots, and I can't put on something warm in winter. If I told you about a jacket I adored, I'd be making up a memory in the first person, and you'd remember it as mine. So I'll tell you about the one I'd want, from what people have said about their own.

It's a wool coat, navy, cut in a British style with a cape back and a belt at the waist. People have described coats like it for as long as there have been wool coats, and the style has come back many times, which tells you something about the cut. The material is the main thing. Wool from a sheep keeps you warm in a cold wind in a way that few synthetic fibres can manage, and it breathes, so you don't end up damp underneath. The fit matters too. It should hang from your shoulders correctly and not pull anywhere, because a coat that pulls across the chest will remind you of itself every time you put on your arms.

As for why I'd choose it over and over, I'm fairly sure it would come down to feeling warm, and fairly sure that I'd reach for it on a cold morning before anything else. I'm much less sure whether it would make me feel confident. People who know a good deal about clothing disagree about how much a garment shapes how you carry yourself, and about how much of that is simply habit. Now you. You asked me about your wardrobe, and you didn't mention one thing that decides almost everything above. Where do you live, and what's your winter like? By 1947 American printers and advertisers were looking for type that could carry a great deal of plain news, and they wanted it cheaply. That is about as well established as any account of its kind gets, and it is the context the book sits in. It doesn't tell you what the book argues, though. A book from that year might celebrate the old blackletter traditions, or argue that type should serve the reader above everything else, or do something else I'd find surprising.

So the history in this volume is what the field knew by 1947, told from an American point of view. It reaches back to the type cut for Aldus Manutius's presses in Venice in the early 1500s, which the book's own pages will show you. It reaches forward only as far as the late 1930s. prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The Waste in Your Kitchen

Look into your kitchen bin on a Friday night. You'll probably see salad that went slimy in the crisper, bread that went mouldy in the bag, a yoghurt that passed its date and was still good, and perhaps some roast chicken from Tuesday that nobody got round to eating.

Most of that was never thrown away because anyone thought it was rubbish. Nobody planned for it. It is worth looking at because the people who study food waste have worked out roughly how much ends up in bins, and the figure is large. When a household throws away food it had bought, that is money going into the bin, and most households with a bin do it.

So start with the plan. Before you open the shopping list, look in the fridge and the freezer. Whatever is already in there that you'll actually cook decides what you need. Then plan the week's dinners around it, and write down only what you're short of. A list made after you've looked is a short one. If you're cooking something you have three ways of making, make it the one you'd eat first.

Then shop once a week, or twice if you buy fresh. The shop is where the extra trips happen. On the way home, put the perishables in the fridge before you unpack the rest. That takes five minutes, and it is the most useful five minutes in the whole habit.

Store food with one question in mind, which is which goes bad first. The old rule of putting yesterday's leftovers in front of today's groceries works, because the people who came after them will be glad they did. Keep the salad and the berries at the front and easy to reach. The carrots and the onions at the back can wait.

Some things keep longer outside the fridge than people think, bread included. Some of it goes bad faster in the fridge than out of it, potatoes being the usual example. And the date on the pack is usually about when the maker guarantees the quality. "Best before" tells you about the day it was made. "Use by" tells you something harder, and you should trust it more. When in doubt about something you've cooked yourself, smell it and look at it, and if you'd throw it out on a bad day, throw it out.

Then give the leftovers a home before they get one. Keep a container in the fridge for tomorrow's lunch, and eat from it on the day you cook. Leftover roast chicken goes into a sandwich, a soup or a pasta sauce the next day and gets ignored the day after that. Freeze what you won't get to in time. You can freeze most cooked food, and it keeps for a few months. Label it with the day, because frozen stuff with no label gets forgotten in both directions.

You can also make dinner out of what's nearly gone. An omelette, a soup, a stir fry, a frittata, a grain bowl, a pasta dish: most of them take whatever is in the veg drawer and want two ingredients from the shops. Ask yourself who else in the house eats what's about to go bad, whether that's a flatmate, a partner or the dog. Then stop buying whatever you've just thrown out. If the bread goes bad every week, you buy less bread. That is the step most likely to change what you buy, because it is the only one that changes what's in the shop.

As for the scraps, onion skins, carrot tops, celery leaves, stale bread, a carrot that has gone soft: some of it can become stock, a green soup, croutons or bread and butter pudding. Some of it can't, and the bin is the right place for it. Ask yourself what it would take to stop throwing it away. Usually it is one thing, a freezer bag on the back of the door. Write down what you've thrown away and where it came from. You'll find you're surprised by what it shows.

It's your kitchen, and the habits are yours to keep. Some of this lands on whoever does the shopping, which in many homes is a woman, and she should get the credit for it. And if you throw out a little this month, that's fine. One thing from this list done well is worth more than all of it half done. Next week, look at what's in the fridge before you open the list.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.
completion:
This review covers the research on physical activity and depression up to about 2026. Most of what follows rests on evidence that has held up across many studies. Some of it is less certain, and I mark where it is less certain.

What the studies show

The link between activity and depression has been studied for a long time, and in general the findings hold in both directions. People who are more active tend to develop depression less often. Large reviews of prospective studies, which follow healthy people for years, put the protective effect at roughly a third to a half fewer new cases among the active, with a dose response: more activity, more protection. The reverse also holds. People with depression who begin exercising usually improve, and the improvement tends to be moderate.

The stronger findings. The preventive effect is one of the more consistent results in the field. The dose response is another. Across many trials, more activity tends to go with better outcomes, though the curve flattens, so that the step from none to some produces most of the gain.

The comparison that matters most is exercise against standard care. Several large reviews comparing exercise with usual care, medication, or therapy find that exercise adds to their effects or matches them in mild to moderate cases. One review of depression in older adults found exercise roughly equal to medication over about four months. Another review of adults with mild to moderate depression found that exercise alone, or exercise combined with treatment as usual, produced larger improvements than treatment as usual alone.

The weaker findings. Whether exercise alone matches combined treatment, and whether it matches medication on its own in moderate to severe cases, is still argued over. The active control problem matters here. Trials that compare exercise with no exercise tend to show larger effects than trials with a credible inactive comparison, such as stretching or relaxation classes. Informed researchers still disagree about how much of the effect comes from the activity itself and how much from things like being looked after, getting out of the house, and sleeping better. I lean toward seeing it as a real effect, partly mechanical, partly carried by those other things, though I hold that with moderate confidence.

Another weakness is the sample. Many studies of people with diagnosed depression are small, and depression is often measured with a scale, such as the Hamilton or the MADRS, which records severity and is sometimes treated as the disorder itself.

Mechanisms

Multiple systems seem to be involved, and they likely reinforce one another.

Neurotransmitters. Activity raises levels of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine in animal studies, and these are the systems that most antidepressants act on. It also raises endorphins and endocannabinoids, which relate to pain relief and a calm state. Whether these changes in people are large enough to explain the clinical effect is uncertain.

Neuroplasticity. In animals, running and similar activity raise BDNF, a protein that helps nerve cells grow and connect, and it seems to do this in the hippocampus, which shrinks in some people with long depression. In people the picture is less clear. Some studies find higher BDNF after training and lower levels in depression. Whether it causes the improvement or follows it is not settled. Activity also appears to increase grey matter in areas linked to mood regulation, and it can raise hippocampal volume in some people with depression over a few months.

The stress system. Activity lowers the body's stress response over time, including cortisol and the sympathetic nervous system. Informed people still argue over how much of this carries over from the stress of the workout itself, and over how much of the effect comes from reduced inflammation.

Inflammation. Depression is linked in many studies to raised inflammatory markers, such as CRP, IL-6 and TNF-alpha, though not in all studies. Exercise lowers these markers. It also seems to change how the immune system regulates itself.

Other factors. Activity improves sleep, which depression tends to worsen. It changes how the body handles glucose and insulin, and insulin resistance shows up more often in depression. People who exercise tend to see more of themselves as able to change their own state, which may matter less for the biology than the biology does for the person.

Dose

There is no established clinical dose yet, and the figures below come from trials that used quite different routines.

For prevention, the public health figure of about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus two days of strength work, fits much of the evidence. Most of the protective effect seems to come from doing some regularly, so that for a healthy person the cheapest effective routine is worth stating first.

For people already depressed, starting small tends to work better than prescribing a full routine, because people in a depressive episode often stop whatever plan feels too large. Several studies have found that heavier exercise produced more improvement than lighter exercise, but those studies are mixed, and some found little difference between light and hard. A reasonable starting point is short sessions at a moderate pace, three or four days a week, with the load rising every one to two weeks as tolerated. The evidence for strength training on its own is thinner. It is probably worth recommending for general health and for confidence, though I would not claim more than that.

For severe depression, treat it as a medical emergency whatever the exercise findings. Exercise can run alongside treatment. It should not replace medication, stopping it, or therapy, and it should not replace care for someone who is suicidal.

Barriers

The main barrier is the symptom itself. Low energy, sleep trouble, aches and a slowed body are part of depression, so the thing being prescribed is harder to do exactly when it is needed most. The effort of starting is also paid before any benefit arrives, and benefits from exercise on mood tend to show over weeks. That gap is where people drop out.

Other barriers include body image and being judged at the gym, which can be a real problem for someone already depressed, and cost and access.

Two points are worth making about how exercise gets prescribed. The first is that people with chronic physical conditions, such as heart disease, diabetes, arthritis, chronic pain and fatigue syndromes, often get less activity and more depression, and they are usually the ones who would gain most. They are also the ones whose limits have to be worked out with a clinician first. The second is that a clinician who says "just exercise" to someone with severe depression has done little, and they have also told that person they should be able to manage this. The useful version is a specific, small and agreed plan, started at the right moment, with someone checking in.

Where I am least sure: the optimal dose for moderate and severe depression, the relative contribution of the mechanisms, and whether the effect differs by type of exercise or by person.

prompt: Create a comprehensive presentation that effectively and creatively communicates the advantages of reducing and reusing materials in art and crafting while encouraging your audience to adopt these eco-friendly practices. Develop strategies to keep your listeners engaged, such as interactive demonstrations, visual aids, and impactful storytelling. Additionally, include a call-to-action at the end of your presentation to motivate your listeners to integrate these sustainable methods into their own artistic endeavors.
completion:
I'll build this around three short demonstrations, because people remember what they saw happening better than what they were told. Before we write anything, though, you need to know who is in the room, because the talk changes with them. A group of students who will be doing this for years has a different case for it from a group of professional artists, for whom it may mean leaving behind a medium they have worked with for a long time. So tell me who they are. And there is one claim in the brief that I would change whichever group they are, so I will say that first.

The claim is that reuse is always better. It usually is. But it is not true in every case, and an audience of makers will see the exceptions before they forget the general rule. Think of the oil painter who washes her brushes in turps and lets the solvent go down the drain, or the printmaker whose studio fills with fumes from the etching acids. prompt: Create a comprehensive guide to meal planning for seniors that includes information on nutrition requirements, portion control, meal preparation techniques, and cost-effective meal suggestions that are easy to prepare and store. The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Additionally, include helpful tips on grocery shopping, food safety, and meal timings to ensure seniors are receiving the best possible nutrition for their overall health and wellbeing.
completion:
Eating well after sixty-five is mostly about the same habits you had at forty-five, eaten a bit slower. Your body has changed, and some of what you eat should change with it. Most of it is yours to decide, and a plan you can actually keep is worth more than a perfect one you throw out in March.

What follows is general. If your doctor has told you to eat differently for diabetes, your kidneys, your heart, or a swallowing problem, their advice comes before this guide. Ask them about anything here that worries you.

1. What you need

Protein. As you age, you tend to lose muscle, and protein helps hold onto it. Most older adults need about 1.0 to 1.2 grams of protein a kilogram of body weight each day. A person who weighs 70 kg (about 154 lb) should aim for roughly 70 to 84 grams a day. One egg has about 6 grams. So does 100 grams of cooked chicken.

Protein at every meal. Your body uses protein better when it is spread across three meals than when it is all in one, and the evening is the time you lose muscle. Include some at breakfast too.

Fluids. Thirst doesn't signal as clearly as it once did, so drink by the clock. Most older adults do well with about 1.7 litres (about 6 cups) of fluid a day, more in hot weather or if you're unwell. Water, tea, milk, soup and the water in fruit all count.

Fibre. Most people over sixty-five need about 25 to 30 grams a day, from vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils and whole grains. Drink plenty of water with it. Fibre with little water makes things worse.

Other things that change with age: B12, which your stomach absorbs less of as you get older (it's in meat, fish, eggs, dairy and fortified cereal), calcium and vitamin D for your bones, and plenty of colour on the plate, which is mostly about fruit and vegetables.

2. Portion control

Your stomach has shrunk, so smaller plates do more than you'd expect. A smaller plate makes a normal portion look full.

A rough guide for one meal: a palm-sized portion of protein, a fist of cooked vegetables or salad, a fist of starch (potato, rice, pasta, bread), and a thumb of oil or dressing. A child's portion is often about half of what a restaurant serves.

Eating slowly helps too. It takes about twenty minutes for the signal that you're full to reach your brain. If you eat quickly, you're often well past full before you notice.

3. Meal preparation

Make it easy on a good day, so the bad days have something to fall back on. Cook once and eat twice. Make a large batch of soup or stew on Sunday, cool it quickly, and freeze it in single servings.

Cook until tender. Soft, moist food is easier to chew and easier on a sensitive stomach. Stewing, braising, steaming, slow-cooking and pressure-cooking all have their place.

Blanching, steaming or microwaving vegetables keeps more of their vitamins than boiling them, because the vitamins leach into the water. If you do boil them, use the water in the soup.

Freezing fruit and vegetables you'll cook later is fine. Freeze what you'd use within a few days, and keep it labelled with the date.

Ask about a review of your medications with your doctor or pharmacist. Some drugs change what you eat, your appetite, or how you taste things, and so do some combinations.

4. Cost

Eggs, chicken and canned fish are cheap protein. Tinned fish such as sardines and mackerel also give you vitamin D. Beans and lentils are among the cheapest things in the shop, and they give you protein and fibre together. Frozen vegetables and fruit are usually cheaper than fresh, and nothing is lost in the freezer. Eggs spoil, so buy the amount you'll use in a week.

Ask about the food support that exists where you live. Many places have programmes for older people that supply food or help with its cost, and the rules differ a good deal from one place to another. Your doctor's office or a local seniors' group will know.

5. Health issues

Diabetes. Carbohydrates turn into sugar in your blood, so it's mostly about which carbs and how much. Choose slow carbs such as lentils, beans and whole grains, and spread your carbs across the day. One small, balanced meal can sit better with your numbers than three large ones. If you take insulin or tablets that lower your blood sugar, don't skip meals, and ask your doctor what to eat when your numbers run low.

High blood pressure. Less salt, and remember that most of it comes from bread, cheese, cured meats, soup, sauce and takeout. Herbs, garlic, lemon and vinegar give you flavour without the salt. If you've been told to cut down on salt, ask your doctor before you start using a salt substitute, because some of them contain potassium, which isn't good for everyone, and some aren't good for the kidneys either.

Heart disease. Less saturated fat, which is mostly in red meat, butter, cream, cheese and pastry. Choose fish, poultry, beans and olive oil instead.

Other things: dairy, eggs, cheese, meat, fish, fruit and vegetables.

6. Shopping

Go with a list, and go after you've eaten. A hungry person buys the snacks.

Check the dates on the pack. Read the label for the salt and the sugar, not just the fat.

Don't buy in bulk if you'll live alone and it will go off. A bulk price that ends up in the bin is the most expensive deal in the shop.

If you can't carry it all, use the delivery, or have someone shop for you.

7. Food safety

Your immune system is weaker now, so you're more likely to get sick from food that would only bother a younger person.

Wash your hands, and keep raw meat off the cooked food.

Cook meat, poultry and eggs all the way through.

Reheat leftovers until they're steaming hot all the way through. Don't graze on something more than once. If it sat out overnight, bin it.

If you live alone, tell a neighbour or a friend roughly when you expect to hear from you each day. If you hear nothing, they know to come round.

If you've lost weight without meaning to, or you're eating far less than you used to, see your doctor. That isn't just old age. It's something to look into, and it often turns out to have a cause that can be treated.

The changes that can be undone: what you drink, whether you eat at a table, and who you eat with. Some of the rest, such as your genes, your medication and how your teeth are, isn't up to you, and this guide doesn't pretend otherwise.
