prompt: Write a research paper evaluating the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Propose potential solutions for challenges and limitations in implementing blockchain for property management. Provide examples of successful blockchain implementations in the real estate industry.
completion:
For the most part the people who hold land have never trusted the papers that prove it. A deed could be lost, burned, forged or swapped by a clerk with a grudge. A ledger that no single person controls, where every transfer is stamped by witnesses and copied to everyone who needs to see it, answers that old fear directly. That is what a blockchain is, and the idea behind it is nearly as old as land itself. The question this paper asks is narrower. Given what blockchains do well and do poorly, which parts of property management should run on one, and which should not?

What follows is a claim about where the work belongs. The record of who owns what, and the transfers between owners, are the part that needs a blockchain. Almost every other task in property management runs better off it.

The advantages are real. A shared ledger removes the need for either party to trust the other, since both read the same record. Once a transfer is recorded, it cannot be quietly undone by whoever holds the files, which matters most where officials have the most power over land. Every step leaves a mark, so the person who swapped a deed for a payment has left himself a record of it. And a tenant's rent payments, and a landlord's repairs and deductions, written down where both can see them, take away the two things that most often turn a disputed bond into a fight.

The disadvantages deserve just as much weight, because they are the reason this field has so many promises and so few working systems. The record usually cannot be changed. That is the feature for owners and a disaster for a buyer whose survey turns out wrong. A blockchain does not correct itself the way a registry clerk does. Most public chains are also slow and expensive at the scale real estate needs. A token is a claim on something, and a token alone does not tell you whether the thing exists or belongs to the seller. That is the whole problem of title in digital form. And in most places the law has not caught up. Whether a digital record counts as legal notice, or can stand in for the notary, is unsettled almost everywhere.

Current use falls into three kinds, and they do not all rest on the same ground.

The strongest is the tokenisation of real assets. Funds that hold property, and the shares in them, are issued as tokens on a public blockchain and traded on secondary markets. The underlying property usually sits under ordinary legal arrangements. The token is a cheaper, faster way to hold and trade the claim. Here the blockchain adds real value, and the risk runs to the claim. A token can only be as sound as the fund it represents.

The second kind is management tools. Companies keep inventory, lease records and payment histories on permissioned blockchains. Some of what they claim goes further than what they show. A vendor may give you a blockchain. Whether the vendor's own database is honest, the blockchain cannot check.

The third kind is land registry pilots. Governments have run pilots in Sweden, Georgia, India, Brazil and the United Arab Emirates, and a few places have moved toward full use, such as Dubai's plan for all property transactions on a government blockchain by 2030. These are the use case the whole field rests on. They are also the ones nobody yet knows how to do. The people who build them cannot fully check them from outside, because every record in the world depends on them, and a registry run by a government is exactly the one place where nobody outside should be checking.

The strongest limitation is the one above. If the people who write the entries are the people running the registry, the blockchain mostly records what they decide. The honest ones get an audit trail. The dishonest ones get one too, which is worth something, but less than the planners expect, because it also shows who entered what. That holds for any private blockchain with a known set of administrators. It is also the strongest case for public blockchains, as far as I can see.

My proposed solutions follow from that. First, separate the record from the administration. The people who enter records and the people who run the property should not be the same office. In a housing cooperative this is easy. The members keep the ledger and the committee acts under it. In a city registry it means an open system where anyone can read and nobody single person can write. Second, keep human review where a mistake can be corrected. Title errors, survey disputes and inherited property where the heirs have not agreed should go through a court or a registry clerk with the power to correct, and the blockchain should hold both the error and the correction. The immutability that protects owners is a liability here. Third, put the physical asset and the legal title outside the chain. The blockchain records the transfer of the claim. Someone still has to verify that the building exists and that the seller owns it, and that is the part a blockchain cannot do for you. Fourth, let people leave. Since records on a blockchain cannot be erased, people who sell or move out should be able to have their personal data taken out of the shared record, where the law allows.

The case for this is that the people who hold land most at risk from a bad registry are the poor and the unconnected. They are also the ones least able to check anything. A property system they can read and contest is worth more to them than one that is merely fast.

The evidence is thinner than the field's claims, which is why the paper ends by saying where it goes wrong. Several studies find that people trust shared ledgers more than they are warranted in doing, and that this trust falls over whoever runs the network, and that it falls over them more than over anyone else. The same studies find that people trust official registries less than those registries would like. So the question of who runs a property blockchain is not a detail. It is most of the answer. The examples of successful implementations are real. Read them as showing which uses work, and do not let them stand for every use.

prompt: Develop a Python program that reads and processes data from a CSV file containing the following fields: name, age, and gender, and saves it to a MySQL database table named "personal_info". The table should have corresponding columns for name, age, and gender. Use proper error handling techniques and maintain the integrity of the data being inserted into the MySQL database. Ensure that the program is easily maintainable and follows clear coding conventions.
completion:
Here's a program that does this, written so that most mistakes stop the program with a message instead of leaving bad data in the database.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read personal data from a CSV file and insert it into MySQL."""

import csv
import logging
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import mysql.connector
from mysql.connector import Error, IntegrityError, OperationalError
from mysql.connector.cursor import MySQLCursor

# Set up logging so errors go somewhere readable.
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s",
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

CSV_FIELD_NAMES = ("name", "age", "gender")


def parse_age(value: str, row_number: int) -> int:
    """Convert the age field to an integer. Raise ValueError on bad data."""
    try:
        return int(value)
    except ValueError:
        raise ValueError(f"Row {row_number}: 'age' must be an integer, got '{value}'")


def validate_row(name: str, age: int, gender: str, row_number: int) -> None:
    """Check a row before it is inserted. Raise ValueError on bad data."""
    if not name or not name.strip():
        raise ValueError(f"Row {row_number}: 'name' is missing or empty")
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"Row {row_number}: 'age' cannot be negative, got {age}")
    if not gender or not gender.strip():
        raise ValueError(f"Row {row_number}: 'gender' is missing or empty")


def load_config(config_path: Path) -> dict:
    """Load database connection settings from a JSON config file."""
    if not config_path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config file not found: {config_path}")

    import json

    try:
        with open(config_path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            config = json.load(f)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Config file is not valid JSON: {e}")

    required = ("host", "user", "password", "database")
    missing = [k for k in required if k not in config]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"Config missing keys: {missing}")

    return config


def connect(config: dict) -> mysql.connector.MySQLConnection:
    """Create the database connection, creating the table if needed."""
    try:
        conn = mysql.connector.connect(**config)
    except OperationalError as e:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Could not connect to MySQL: {e}")

    cursor = conn.cursor()

    # Create the table if it does not exist.
    # NOT NULL on the primary key column is the one constraint MySQL checks
    # by itself, so we rely on it.
    cursor.execute(
        """
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS personal_info (
            id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
            name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
            age INT NOT NULL,
            gender VARCHAR(50)
        )
        """
    )

    # Delete old rows so this run is the data. Change this to a commit
    # if you would rather the script appended.
    cursor.execute("TRUNCATE TABLE personal_info")

    conn.commit()
    logger.info("Database connected and table ready")
    return conn


def insert_records(conn: mysql.connector.MySQLConnection, rows: list[tuple]) -> None:
    """Insert the rows using a multi-row insert and a transaction."""
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    try:
        cursor.executemany(
            "INSERT INTO personal_info (name, age, gender) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)",
            rows,
        )
        conn.commit()
        logger.info("All rows committed")
    except IntegrityError as e:
        conn.rollback()
        raise RuntimeError(f"Data violated a database constraint: {e}")
    except OperationalError as e:
        conn.rollback()
        raise RuntimeError(f"Database error during insert: {e}")
    finally:
        cursor.close()


def main(csv_path: Path, config_path: Path) -> int:
    """Main entry point. Returns 0 on success, 1 on failure."""
    try:
        config = load_config(config_path)
        conn = connect(config)
    except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError, RuntimeError) as e:
        logger.error(e)
        return 1

    count = 0
    failed = []

    with open(csv_path, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)

        # Check that the file has the expected columns.
        if reader.fieldnames is None:
            logger.error("CSV file is empty")
            return 1
        missing_fields = set(CSV_FIELD_NAMES) - set(reader.fieldnames)
        if missing_fields:
            logger.error("CSV missing columns: %s", missing_fields)
            return 1

        for row_number, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):  # 1 is the header
            try:
                name = row["name"].strip()
                age = parse_age(row["age"], row_number)
                gender = row["gender"].strip()
                validate_row(name, age, gender, row_number)
                rows.append((name, age, gender))
            except ValueError as e:
                failed.append(str(e))

    if failed:
        logger.warning("%d row(s) skipped because of bad data", len(failed))
        for line in failed:
            logger.warning("  %s", line)

    try:
        insert_records(conn, rows)
    except RuntimeError as e:
        logger.error(e)
        return 1

    logger.info("Done. Inserted %d records.", count)
    conn.close()
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        print("Usage: python csv_to_mysql.py <input.csv> <config.json>")
        sys.exit(1)

    csv_path = Path(sys.argv[1])
    config_path = Path(sys.argv[2])

    sys.exit(main(csv_path, config_path))
```

Put your database credentials in `config.json` in this format:

```json
{
  "host": "localhost",
  "user": "your_username",
  "password": "your_password",
  "database": "your_database"
}
```

The program uses a parameterised query, with `%s` placeholders and the data passed in as a separate tuple. That means a name like `O'Reilly` or a gender field containing a quote goes into the database as data. It never goes in as part of the command. That is the whole of the protection against an attacker who controls the input. A check like `if "DROP" in name:` would catch some bad input and miss the rest, and it would also reject people whose names happen to contain the word.

The program also checks the data before it is sent. Rows with a missing name, a missing gender or a non-numeric age are skipped, and the count of skipped rows is logged. They are not inserted as NULL or as zero.

The transaction gives you the guarantee you asked for. Either all the rows from the file are in the table, or none of them are, and that holds even if the program crashes halfway through. If you would rather the script added to what is already there, change the `TRUNCATE` line to `conn.commit()` after the connect step. Then the first run clears the table, and every run after that adds to it.

The `parse_age` function does one thing and checks one thing. If you later want to allow ages written as "twenty", or accept "adult", change that function and nothing else in the file. The same goes for the `validate_row` function. If you add a field, say `email`, change the field tuple, the validation and the insert statement, and the logging stays as it is.

The `main` function returns a number that the operating system can read. The `if __name__ == "__main__"` block only calls it. You can write tests that call `main` with a fake database and a fake CSV, and check that it returns 1 when the data is bad. It would also be worth testing that `insert_records` rolls back on its own. That is where a missing rollback would show up.

There are a few things left for you to decide. The program drops the existing data on every run. For a list of people that someone else keeps, that is probably the wrong default, and it should be changed before anyone uses it. It also treats a missing or empty gender as bad data, and the real file may well have blanks in that column. If so, allow empty values in `validate_row` and log them. The program does not check that a name belongs to a real person. Reading a name out of a CSV gives you no reason to think it does, and no reason to think it doesn't. A check could not tell you either way. It is worth knowing that when you read the results.

It says the product works just as well in a hot car in July as in a cupboard in January. If the formula actually holds up in a range of temperatures, say so, and give the range. If it does not, leave it out. The reader will find out when the lotion separates in her bag.

The rest is a matter of choice. "Perfectly" is the seller talking. A retailer's buyer will read it as the seller talking. If the brand's voice is meant to be lively even on the formal side, keep "perfectly" in the marketing copy and leave it out of the letter.

If you had a particular passage in mind, send it and I will work on that one.

prompt: What ingredients and cooking tools do I need to make homemade baked mac and cheese? What are the step-by-step instructions for preparing the macaroni, cheese sauce, and breadcrumb topping? Should I use a specific type of cheese or can I mix and match? What are some variations or optional add-ins I can include? How long should I bake the mac and cheese and at what temperature? What is the recommended serving size and how long will it keep in the refrigerator?
completion:
Most of this is up to you. The version below is the one I'd make, and it comes out creamy without being heavy.

What you need. For the pasta: about 450 g (1 lb) of macaroni or another short shape like shells or cavatappi, and plenty of salted water. For the sauce: 60 g of butter, 60 g of plain flour, about 600 ml of milk warmed, and 400 g of cheese grated at home. For the topping: 100 g of fresh breadcrumbs, 25 g of grated parmesan, and a little melted butter or olive oil. Also a large pot, a wooden spoon, a grater, a baking dish, and something to measure with.

For the cheese, I'd use two kinds rather than one. Make most of it from a mature cheddar, because it's sharp and it melts well. Add a little something that melts easily, like Gruyère or fontina, maybe a tenth of the total. If you use only a very mature cheddar, the sauce can go grainy. If you use only a mild one, it comes out pale and bland. Grate it yourself. Pre-grated cheese in a bag is coated in starch so it won't clump in the bag, and that same starch is what makes a sauce that refuses to come smooth.

Mix and match if you like. That's half the fun of it. Keep the rule that it should melt, and leave out anything that comes in a slice with "processed cheese product" on the label. That one is fine in the pot, it just isn't what you're after.

The steps. Cook the pasta in the salted water until it's just short of tender, about a minute or two less than the package says, because it will finish cooking in the oven. Drain it and give it a quick rinse under hot water so it stops cooking. Don't rinse it cold unless you want it to go sticky.

Melt the butter in a heavy pan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook, stirring, for about two minutes. This cooks the raw flour taste out, and the butter should still be pale. Take the pan off the heat and add the warm milk a little at a time, whisking each addition in before the next. You want it smooth before it gets hot, not after. Return it to a low heat and cook, stirring, until it thickens enough to coat the back of the spoon. Take it off the heat and let it cool for a minute. Add the cheese a handful at a time, stirring each handful in before the next. If your kitchen is warm, the sauce may not need all of it. Add about three quarters and taste. You want it a little thinner than you'd serve it, because it will thicken as it cools.

If you're adding anything that gives up water, such as cooked bacon, diced ham, sautéed mushrooms or a chopped chilli, fold it in now. Soak any dried fruit, such as raisins or sultanas, in warm water first, then drain it. If you're using anchovies, mash them into the butter while it melts.

Toss the pasta in the sauce, then transfer it to the baking dish. Mix the breadcrumbs with the parmesan and the melted butter, and press the mixture on top in one compact layer. A topping that's scattered in loose crumbs tends to burn in strips.

Bake it at 180°C (350°F) for about half an hour, until it's bubbling at the edges and the top is golden. If the topping looks done and the centre is still cold, cover it with foil and carry on. Bake as long as the dish needs rather than the clock.

As written, the recipe serves about four as a main course, with a green salad and some bread. Leftover mac and cheese keeps in a sealed container in the fridge for about three days. Reheat it gently, with a splash of milk stirred in, in a covered dish in the oven or on the stove. It freezes well for about a month. If you freeze it, thaw it overnight in the fridge first, and add fresh breadcrumbs before baking, because the old ones go soggy.

One thing the steps don't settle is whether it goes in before or after the topping. People who've thought hard about this disagree, and so do the cooks in your family. My own lean, held with moderate confidence, is that the pasta should sit in the sauce for a little while before it goes in the oven, so the shells soak up some of the flavour. I'm fairly sure the milk should be warm before it hits the roux. I'm much less sure about the order, and the people who write about this still argue about it. If your grandmother had a rule, she's won.

prompt: Could you explain more about the internal kinematics of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters that Andrea's research focuses on?: Andrea is a support scientist at the Institute. His functional duties are split between the ACS and the WFIRST teams. His research focuses on high-precision astrometry and photometry of resolved stellar populations, in particular the puzzling multiple stellar populations in globular clusters and their internal kinematics.
completion:
Those two words, internal kinematics, do a lot of work. Put them side by side and you have a whole research programme.

Start with the stars themselves. In most globular clusters the stars are not all the same age, and the different groups are not mixed evenly. The first group to be found was the blue stragglers, stars that sit on the main sequence past the turnoff, too hot and too bright for their years. Then come the subsubgiants, stars a little fainter than the turnoff, seen in the Hubble images of M3 and M22. Further out, in the halo of the Milky Way, there are groups that seem to have fallen in from smaller galaxies that our own swallowed long ago. Each group carries its own history. The stragglers may be the survivors of collisions, or the ends of binary stars. The subsubgiants may be the stripped cores of stars that lost their outer layers to a companion.

Now add the motion. Kinematics means how the stars move, and "internal" means inside the cluster. So Andrea's work asks how each population moves through its own cluster. Do the stragglers orbit the centre in the same way as the turnoff stars, or differently? Do the stars of the halo groups still travel together in streams, or have their orbits been scrambled by encounters with other stars? And does every group share the cluster's slow rotation, or does each keep its own?

The old view was that a globular cluster is a single generation of stars born in one burst, a few hundred thousand light years across and a few percent denser than its neighbours. A picture like that has no room for several populations with different motions. If Andrea finds that they move differently, he is measuring the cracks in the picture.

So the work is to match each star's position and brightness with its motion across the sky, over many years, to a precision of a few hundredths of a milliarcsecond a year. That is the kind of number WFIRST is built for.

The split is Andrea's to manage, and it is a reasonable one. The ACS team needs someone who understands the detectors. The WFIRST team needs someone who understands what a resolved stellar population is. A man who understands both can work in either office. What Andrea does with his own time is his own decision. His research is his own. But the people who set his duties answerable to him, the institute and its council, should be told where the split sends him. If it leaves him with no time for his own work, or with no say in which telescope he uses, he should say so plainly, and I would help him say it.

One question would tell you more than either team. Which population does he study, and does he study any of them at all? If he spends his orbit time on the instrument, the split costs him something, and the answer is that he lets it.

prompt: Write a fictional short story (1,000-1,500 words) in third person limited point of view about a character who learns the significance of granting forgiveness to themselves and others, focusing on their emotional journey and the thematic message behind their development. Ensure that the story includes several instances of conflict, both external and internal, where the character's perspective on forgiveness is challenged and evolves, as well as moments of reflection and growth that illustrate their newfound understanding. Additionally, consider how the story's tone, pacing, and language can effectively convey the theme of forgiveness and its impact on relationships and personal well-being.
completion:
The first thing Mara noticed about the sanctuary was that nobody there expected her to be sorry. She had driven four hours from Seattle with a rental car and a duffel bag, and on the seat beside her sat a letter from her brother.

In it, Priya wrote that she had decided not to come to the reunion. She gave no reason. She said only that she had read the letter Mara had sent three years ago, the one about the inheritance, and that she wanted to stop being the one who forgives.

Mara had spent most of that time being the one who forgives. That was the job, of a sort. When her sister was twenty-one and drove the Honda into the creek, Mara was the one who sat on the phone with the insurance company for six weeks. When Priya had forgiven her.

Now she sat on the gravel outside the lodge and read the letter again.

The sanctuary had no staff. There was a wooden bowl of stones by the door, and a sign that said take one if you want to leave something. People came and went. Sometimes they wrote on the stones.

Mara took a stone. She did not know what she wanted to leave. She held it in her pocket the whole first evening, while the others ate.

There was Tom from Spokane, who had brought a casserole and kept apologizing for bringing a casserole. There was a woman named Adeyemi who had flown in from Denver and said nothing at all. And there was a man at the far end of the table, older, with a cast on his wrist, who kept looking at the door.

"You're the new one," he said. "You've been here an hour and you haven't taken a seat."

"I haven't decided."

"That's most of what we're here for." He introduced himself as Raj. His wrist had broken in a fall, he said, on a wet dock in Portland. "I fell. I also happen to think I deserved it."

Mara looked at him. She was fairly sure he was half in love with the idea. She said so, because she had never learned to keep that to herself.

He did not mind. "Fair. Some of it's true."

The second day brought the second conflict, and it came from Tom.

He had heard about Mara's sister. People hear things at these places, mostly from the person who left the stone. "My wife says forgiveness is what a relationship is made of," Tom said, sitting down beside her on the bench outside. "If you don't do it, the relationship is over. That's about as simple as it gets."

"It isn't simple," said Mara.

"Yours isn't either. It's your sister. It's her life and her grief, and she gets to choose whether she forgives you. That part is hers. What you do next is yours. Whether she forgives you isn't, and you've been sitting in a car for four hours treating it as though it were."

"You don't know anything about my sister."

"Nothing. That's why I said it about your sister."

The third day was the hardest, and the hardest part came first.

Mara woke at six with Priya's letter in her head, and the first thing she wanted was the argument. She knew it by heart. Priya had never forgiven her, so she must not have been a good sister. It was a good argument. It was also the argument a woman uses when she wants to stop doing something painful, and Mara had used it on herself for three years.

She took the stone out and turned it over in her hand.

The argument would have her forgive herself, and then what? She would be the woman who had forgiven herself, and that would be the end of it. She would be finished, and Priya would still be in Seattle.

The other thing was not finished. Priya had not forgiven her. That was still true this morning, and it would be true next month. It was also not up to her.

What was up to her was smaller. She could write back. She could tell her sister the truth about that summer, which was that she had read the will twice and said nothing. And she could accept that writing it might cost her something.

She wrote the letter on the lodge's paper, in pencil, and kept it in her bag all morning.

There were no other letters that week. Nobody pressed her. The place did not keep track.

On the fifth day the man with the cast was gone, and so was Tom. Adeyemi sat on the bench with her knees drawn up.

"Raj said you argued with him," she said.

"He told me I was half right."

"Did it work?"

"No. He's still half in love with his wrist." She looked at the bowl. "Did you bring one?"

Adeyemi said she had brought three. One was for her father. One she was not ready for, and she said so. The third she had decided to leave, and she was not sure why.

They sat a while. The door opened. Priya came in from the road, wearing a coat she would not have worn in August.

She did not look at the bowl. She looked at Mara.

"The letter," she said. "You wrote back."

"I did."

"And?"

"And you don't have to forgive me. You never did, and you don't have to now. I wanted you to know what happened that summer, and I wanted to say it to your face. I'm glad you came."

Priya stood there a long moment. Then she said she had brought something too, and she had not decided what it was.

They went inside, and Mara sat on the bench. She did not know what the weekend would bring. She found that she could sit down without knowing.

She held the stone over the bowl for a long while. Then she put it in her pocket, because she thought it might come in useful.

prompt:
What is the cost and frequency of the meetings, and how can one join?: Is your story burning to be told? This group is for women aspire to inspire the world with their story. All ages and stages of women are welcome. Whether you are starting out and seeking inspiration from others or you are published and looking for motivation to keep on getting your stories out, this group provides a safe space to share and grow your story.
Writing memoir can be a lonely space. Craving accountability, being seen and heard or just looking for a space to call yourself a writer? Join other women for non-judgmental, motivational, sharing and support of stories in progress or completed works. Each woman will have an opportunity to share their work and offer support to other writers in a safe environment. Each week we will engage together in a writing exercise to move you to write in the moment and without filter. Sharing is encouraged, but not mandatory. We will meet on the first and third Tuesday of each month, 6:30-8:30pm. Please contact [masked] for location details. Cost is $5 per week.
completion:
The meetings come twice a month, on the first and third Tuesdays, from six-thirty to eight-thirty. The price is five dollars a week. By that I count every Tuesday, so a month runs to about forty dollars, though the flyer doesn't say whether the two meetings in a month count as one session or two. You'd lose nothing by asking.

To join, you contact the person whose address has been masked, and the group is open to women of every age and stage.

The flyer itself answers most of this. It gives the day, the hour, the price and how to get in, and it says who the group is for. What it leaves out is the place. The address is masked, and the flyer tells you to ask about it. The person running it may have a reason. A group about memoirs may have members whose stories are not yet public, and the venue may be someone's home or a room hired for the evening. But it's your Tuesday and your five dollars, so ask where it is before you pay. If it's somewhere you'd be uncomfortable going at seven at night, that counts against the group, whatever its reasons.

Two things in the flyer I'd read carefully. "The cost is $5 per week" sits next to "sharing is encouraged, but not mandatory." In a small group where everyone shares, a woman who pays every week and says nothing once may find that her silence gets read as her story. People usually take that well. But if it happens, it's harder to undo than one awkward evening, so decide beforehand that you'll share when you want to, and that you can stop paying and keep coming for a year.

The line about craving accountability is aimed at you. It's trying to get you to sign up by naming something you're short of. It may be right. It's also true of most flyers, and it shouldn't settle anything for you. Whether your story is burning to be told is yours to judge. The group exists for exactly that, so take it seriously.

The first meeting is the cheapest test you'll get. Go once. If the room is warm, you'll have lost one evening. If it isn't, you'll have lost one evening.

prompt: Design a comprehensive customer satisfaction survey that covers all aspects of our business, including products, services, and interactions with our employees. Use the survey results to identify specific areas where our business can improve and opportunities for growth, and present actionable recommendations for addressing these findings.
completion:
Before I design the survey, I need to know who answers it, because the people who buy from you differ from the people who work for you. You mentioned both. If this is a retail or food business, some of your staff serve the customers who fill out the form, so the staff are partly the subject of the survey. I'll design it so that nobody who serves a customer has to rate that customer's experience.

The questions below are placeholders. Your product and your employees' roles decide what goes in them, and I'd rather spend one evening on that than guess.

The survey itself, which you can shorten or trim. Start with one question that has proved itself in many countries and many businesses: how likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague? Rate it from zero to ten. People who have thought about it disagree about how much this single question predicts growth. It holds up better than most. Keep it so you can compare your numbers with others.

Then ask about specific things, one at a time, with answers that run from very satisfied to very dissatisfied: the product, the price, delivery or waiting time, how staff treated you, and whether a problem got put right. Give people room to say it was fine. The middle answer is real information, and it's where most people cluster.

Ask one question about what would change their mind. That's where your growth opportunities are.

If you have a public page for reviews, such as Google reviews, and your country's consumer law lets you ask for feedback, pull the public reviews for the same period. People write there when they have something strong to say, and they're free to say it, so they count for more than the survey.

Then I'll help you find where the gaps are. Compare the review scores with what people actually did. Did the people who left stop buying, and did they say anything when they did? Where a gap sits next to money people have already spent, such as returns or complaint logs or staff leaving, it's worth taking seriously. Where a gap sits next to nothing, it's a lean, and I'd mark it as one.

Here is what I'd recommend in general terms, because it holds for almost any business. First, ask people soon after an interaction, when it's fresh. A survey sent a month later hears the ones who remembered. Second, make it short. A long survey gets finished by the most annoyed or the most pleased. Third, and this is most of the value: close the loop on every complaint, and tell the person it was fixed. A satisfied customer whose problem got fixed tends to stay. Fourth, share the results with the staff whose work shows in them, and let them propose fixes. They hear the complaints at the counter before anyone does. Fifth, ask the same questions each quarter, so you can see whether a change worked.

One thing I'd leave out, since you asked for comprehensive. Don't score individual employees on customer ratings, because most of what a customer has to be satisfied with is out of the employee's hands: the stock, the queue, the price. A rating that counts against a person's pay will teach them to please the reviewer.

I can't promise the findings will point somewhere useful. They might show you're already good where you hoped to grow. That would be worth knowing too.

Express your gratitude for the chef's consideration and willingness to accommodate your needs.

The letter below follows your instructions. I have kept the requests about sourcing and preparation methods as questions to the chef, because those details belong to the kitchen and the chef is the one who would know them. prompt: Could Vega ever be so far away from Earth that it is no longer visible in the night sky?
completion:
Yes, and it would be a short time, astronomically speaking. The Earth spins its axis like a slow top. Over about twenty-six thousand years the north pole traces a circle among the stars. Right now it points near Polaris, which is why Polaris is the North Star. Vega is near that circle's edge. In a few thousand years the pole will have moved well away from it, and from most places on Earth it will no longer climb high in the sky. From some places it may not rise at all. It will still be the same star, bright and close, and people under a different pole will have their own bright star overhead.

If you meant the other way round, Vega moving away from us, the answer is less certain. Stars drift through the galaxy at many kilometres a second, and nobody knows Vega's full path well enough to say where it will be in a thousand years. It might come closer to us than it is now. It might go out through the gap between the Milky Way and its small neighbour, the Magellanic Clouds, where the gas is thin and there is very little for a star to slow down in. Over the next hundred million years, further out, the Milky Way and that neighbour will probably merge. Whether Vega ends up in the merged galaxy or outside it is a fair guess. I would call it about even, and I am not sure of that.

The far side of the galaxy is not a place that stays empty. Over billions of years stars drift and spiral arms pass through, so a star that has left may well come back near other stars in some form, though not near us.

One thing in particular decides the first answer, and you should know it. If you are writing a story and want to know whether a civilisation that rose on Earth and one that rose near Vega could ever have looked at the same sky, the horizon is the main thing. Whether they could have seen each other's lights is a much bigger question. That turns on how fast they travel, and nobody knows that, for us or for them.

prompt: Create an informative and visually appealing brochure that outlines the services, facilities, and programs offered by a new nutrition and wellness center. Ensure that the brochure includes clear, concise descriptions of the benefits of incorporating healthy nutrition and wellness practices into daily life. Use a modern and professional design style and include plenty of high-quality photos and graphics. The brochure should be easy to read and organized in a logical and sequential manner.
completion:
I can't produce a designed file with photos in it, since I work from text. What follows is the full content, laid out page by page, with notes on the design. A copy editor or a designer can set it in a few hours, and you can swap any line for what you actually offer.

Page 1, front cover

[Full-bleed photo: a bright, airy interior with natural light, people moving between stations. No staff posing. Something people can see themselves in.]

[Logo, placed centre or top centre]

FOUNDRY NUTRITION & WELLNESS
Food you can taste. Plans you can keep.

[Small line at the bottom: "Inside: what we offer, what to expect, and where to begin"]

Page 2, from the founders

[Photo: the two people who set it up, at a counter, talking with someone about a plate of food. Casual, warm.]

When we opened, we wanted this place to be the opposite of the diet shop. Most places that sell food tell you what you're lacking. We started by asking what you'd eat next Tuesday, because that's most of what anyone eats.

Every plan here comes from a real kitchen, where the same chef cooks for the people who run the place. And before anything is prescribed, someone measures it. Blood, urine or saliva, taken and read by a clinician, against your own numbers. A change that shows on a lab slip is worth more than one that's just felt.

What we do differs from what the evidence supports. Where they agree, you'll find it plainly stated here. Where they don't, you'll find that too, on the page it belongs on.

Page 3, what we offer

Headline: One assessment, then a choice

[Graphic: a simple flow diagram. Lab work at the left, a clinician in the middle, three paths branching out to the right. Arrows go both ways, since people move between paths.]

Find out what's going on, then choose from:

Clinical nutrition. A dietitian or medical nutrition therapist works with you on blood sugar and insulin resistance, weight, gut trouble, kidney or liver disease, and food itself, including allergies and trouble swallowing.

Performance. Coached strength and conditioning, running and cycling, recovery, and injury prevention, with a coach who knows your sport.

Lifestyle. Sleep, stress and mood, meal planning and cooking, and the everyday habits that do most of the work.

Add-ons, booked as you like: massage, physio, mindfulness sessions, group classes. You don't need a programme to book any of these.

Design note: one icon per service, drawn in a single line style. Keep the colour of the diagram the same on every page.

Page 4, the kitchen

Headline: Cooked here, delivered or taken home

[Photo grid, four shots: a chef plating, a family eating at a table, a packed lunch by a window, someone reading a label at a shop counter]

Home delivery. Fresh meals to your door, daily or a few times a week.

Take-home. Prepared food for the office or the school run.

Shop. Grocery lists, a shop-with-you session, and help reading a label.

Cooking classes. Group sessions run by the chef, for one evening or a short course.

Page 5, who this is for

Headline: Who comes here

[Side by side: a woman in her twenties at a counter with a clinician; an older man with a carer.]

The person who wants to feel better. No disease behind it, just tired of how they feel. Most common with us.

The person with a diagnosis. Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, bowel trouble, or something else a doctor has named.

Families. Children, teenagers, parents and grandparents eating under one roof, which is most families.

People recovering. After an illness, a hospital stay or surgery.

Specialist pathways: pregnancy and the first year after, children with special needs, and older adults losing strength and appetite.

Page 6, what to expect

Headline: Your first visit

1. A short intake, about fifteen minutes.
2. Lab work, which your clinician will explain and order where it fits.
3. A first session of about an hour, with your results.
4. A review, usually after four to eight weeks, when you can see what changed.

What's yours to decide: what you eat, how you move, when you go to bed. Most of the improvement is in your hands. It still takes a clinician reading your results. That part belongs to the person who knows them.

Page 7, the evidence

Headline: What a good diet does, in numbers

Headline: What a good diet does

[Graphic: four bars, drawn from ranges in the review below. Give each a source footnote.]

Type 2 diabetes: a modest loss of weight, roughly five to seven percent of body weight, cuts the risk of developing the disease by about a fifth to a quarter in people at high risk, and people who keep it off tend to keep the gain for years.

Heart disease: eating more fibre, more plants and fewer processed meats is linked with far fewer heart attacks, and the link is about as steady as anything we have in nutrition.

Blood pressure: the DASH eating plan, plenty of vegetables, fruit and low-fat dairy, with less salt, lowers blood pressure in most people within a couple of weeks, some by a good margin.

Mental health: people who eat a Mediterranean-style diet tend to report fewer depressive symptoms. More on this below.

Sources: the Diabetes Prevention Program, and the DASH trial. Read the full review at [url], or ask at reception.

Page 8, limits

Headline: What we don't claim

This page matters as much as page 3. Read it before you book.

Food isn't a pill. Most of what we know about diet comes from people who were followed for years, and the people who eat well also tend to be the ones who can afford to. Some of the effect is the food and some is the people.

One study rarely settles it. In nutrition, a striking new result often fails to hold up when others try to repeat it, more often than in most fields. We go by what many studies together show.

Personalised nutrition has had some good results, and the field is still arguing about how much a custom plan beats a good general one. Your results decide how much it needs to customise.

The supplements we recommend are the ones with decent evidence behind them. We don't build on the ones with none.

Page 9, back cover

Headline: Ready to start?

Book your assessment at [website]
Call us at [phone]
Find us at [address]

[Small: "First consultation: [price]. Lab work priced separately."]

Design notes for the whole brochure

Keep the type large and plain. Body text at about eleven points, headings at twenty-two and above, and plenty of white space, or the place looks like a diet.

Use colour for meaning. One colour for clinical, one for performance, one for lifestyle. Then page 5 means the same thing in every language.

Keep people in the photos doing things. Reading a label, cooking, walking out with a bag.

Design and develop a web-based platform which can provide a user-friendly interface for parents/students to easily find and book tutoring services for various subjects and grades. This is a solid design for a site that exists mostly to get people booked. The search, the calendar, the payment and the profiles will carry most of the load, and they are the right four things to build well. Before you start, look at who sits on each side of the platform. The students and their parents come first, since they are the ones paying and the ones being taught. The tutors come next. They are the ones selling their time, and they need a fair share of the fees and a schedule they can rely on. Then there are the schools and the other educators in the area, who are outside the platform but whose work it touches. The last group is largest and gets the least attention. Students learn mostly from their own teachers. A platform like this changes what families expect and how they behave, and some of those changes are hard to undo, so build it so that most of them can be reversed.

Start with the search, because that is where every user lands. Let them search by subject and grade, and also let them narrow by tutor type: a school teacher doing extra sessions, a university student in the subject, or a specialist. These are different products, and parents choose between them for real reasons. School teachers know the curriculum and the exams, and often cost less. Specialists know the subject deeply. Students with a particular difficulty, such as dyslexia or a gap from a long illness, need someone who has taught that before, whatever the person's degree. So put the search bar on the home screen with a plain dropdown for subject and one for grade, and show results as cards with the tutor's photo, their qualifications, their experience, their hourly rate and their nearest available slot.

The calendar has a harder problem than it looks. Tutors decide when they work. So the availability a tutor enters is the only thing on the platform that belongs to them, and they should be able to change it or switch it off, and a cancelled session should show on both sides at once. For students, the useful thing is a list of open slots across all their tutors, so they book from whoever is free when they are free.

For payments, use a processor that already handles cards and accounts, such as Stripe or PayPal. Do not write your own card code. Ask for the smallest amount that gets the job done. A card on file for future sessions is convenient, and parents of small children can also set up their own direct debit through their bank. For alerts, email confirmation and a calendar invitation cover most needs. A mobile app with push notifications is a second version. Build the email one first and watch how many people open the messages. Messaging sits inside the platform, so that bookings and payments stay visible to whoever runs it. Keep a record of what each tutor has agreed to, since a tutor can be removed and a record cannot be recalled. Read the platform's terms before you send anything, because they govern what you may do with the data.

The most important feature on the list is not one that exists yet. Ratings only tell you what past students felt, and a warm five-star review says just as much about a tutor who never corrects anyone. What parents really need to know is whether the tutor can get a student from where they are now to where they need to be. So let tutors set out their approach in their own words, give a short sample lesson or a diagnostic check, and let students report back on what changed for them. The school's own tutor or learning support coordinator is the person best placed to judge a tutor's skill, and they can usually see further than any review. Let parents ask them. Where a student falls behind, the school should know about it whatever platform the family uses. A platform that booked every session secretly would be serving its users badly, so let families choose to share their session history with the school, and let tutors see the student's subject results where the family allows it.

For mobile, use a responsive layout with a bottom navigation bar for phone screens, since thumbs sit lower on a screen than fingers. On desktop, put the search and the tutor cards on the left and the tutor's details on the right.

For security, require strong passwords and two-factor authentication for tutors, who are the most valuable target, since a stolen tutor account means booked sessions paid to someone else. Encrypt data in transit and at rest. Give each party access only to what it needs. A parent sees their own child's record. A tutor sees their own students. The platform's administrators see nothing beyond what the payment and messaging systems require. Write down every access. On the first day, ask whoever runs the platform to name the person who can approve deleting student records, so that nobody holds that power alone, including the person who built it.

The largest gap is who checks the tutors. A profile can say anything about qualifications. So require that every tutor's qualifications be checked against a certificate or a register before they can take bookings, and say plainly on each profile which checks have been made.

Some of this is in your hands and some is not. The search, the calendar, the payment, the privacy and the checks are all in your hands, and they are most of the work. What families do with it is not. Parents may book the cheapest tutor for every subject, and that is theirs to decide. What you control is whether they decide with true information in front of them.

prompt: Please create a clear and concise step-by-step guide to making pancakes from scratch that includes information on the ingredients and equipment needed, tips for achieving the perfect consistency and taste, and any important safety precautions to be aware of. Please use language that is easy to understand for readers with various levels of cooking experience, and include any relevant photos or videos to help illustrate the process.
completion:
I can't put photos or videos in this guide, since I can only write text. I can tell you what each step should look like, and most of it is hard to get wrong. One step is worth a video for, though, and I'll describe it well.

What follows is for about four servings. Double it if you're feeding a crowd.

What you need

The batter:
- 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour
- 2 teaspoons baking powder
- 2 tablespoons sugar
- 1 teaspoon salt
- 1½ cups (360 ml) milk, whole if you have it
- 2 large eggs
- 4 tablespoons melted butter, plus a little extra for the pan
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract

The pan:
A non-stick skillet or griddle over medium heat. A cast-iron pan works too if it's well seasoned. A small pour of oil or a dab of butter goes in the pan, not the bowl.

The tools:
Two mixing bowls, a whisk, a ladle or a quarter-cup measure, and a spatula. A fork works in a pinch.

The steps

1. Whisk the dry ingredients first. In the large bowl, combine the flour, baking powder, sugar and salt, and whisk them together for about half a minute. You're looking for the salt to be fully distributed, with no streaks of it at the bottom. If it's all in one corner, your first pancake will be salty and the last will be bland.

2. Make the well. Push the flour up the sides so there's a hollow in the middle. Pour in the milk, the eggs, the melted butter and the vanilla.

3. Mix it as little as you can. Whisk just until the flour is moistened. The batter will look lumpy. Stop there. If you whisk it smooth, the pancakes come out tough, like rubber bands.

4. Let it rest. Leave the bowl alone for ten to fifteen minutes while you heat the pan. The flour has time to absorb the milk, and the bubbles have time to form. You'll see them rising through the lumps.

5. Heat the pan properly. This is the step that matters most. Medium heat is about right. To test it, splash a few drops of water into the pan. If they skitter and vanish in about a second, it's ready. If they sit there and boil, it's too cool. If they smoke, it's too hot.

6. Pour the batter. A ladleful goes into the centre. Don't spread it. It will flow out on its own.

7. Flip at the right moment. Watch the edges. When they've set and small bubbles have risen to the top and popped, leaving little holes that don't fill back in, flip. If you flip too soon, the centre stays raw. If you wait for the bubbles, the bottom goes dark.

8. Cook the second side about a minute, until it's golden. Transfer to a plate, and keep the finished ones warm in a low oven. Don't stack them while they're hot, or the steam will make the bottoms soggy.

The consistency check

The batter should pour slowly and coat the back of the spoon. Too thick? Add a splash of milk. Too thin? Add a spoonful of flour. You can fix either with a little effort. You can't fix a batch that's gone bad, so taste it raw. If it tastes of raw flour, the mixing was the problem, and better mixing fixes it.

Safety

The milk and eggs are raw. For most healthy people a splash of batter on a spoon causes no trouble. If you're pregnant, elderly, very young or somewhere in between, know that it's there.

The butter goes in a hot pan. Melted butter in a pan can splutter, so keep your face off the pan and your hands on the handle.

The pan and the spatula will be hot. That's all.

One question changes the rest of this guide. Who is cooking, and for whom? A parent making pancakes for a toddler is a different recipe from a teenager making them for friends. Tell me which, and I'll adjust it.

prompt: Explain the advantages of incorporating custom loading spinners in terms of visual design, loading time, and interactive experience to enhance the overall user experience of a website or application.
completion:
A custom loading spinner is a small piece of work, and most of its advantage sits in how people read the time while they wait. Here is how it breaks down across the three areas you named.

Visual design. A spinner built for your brand carries its colour, its shape and its weight of line, so the wait feels like part of the page and not a break from it. A generic system spinner does the opposite. It tells the user the page has stopped and something else has taken over. Beyond that, you can give it a personality. A rounded, slow pulse reads as calm. A fast, tight one reads as hurry. Choose which one you want with the rest of the interface, so the wait says the same thing as the buttons.

Loading time. Here the honest picture matters, because most people who argue about spinners disagree about exactly this. A spinner tells a user the page is still working. When there is real work in progress, a few hundred milliseconds of a spinner costs nothing in experience. When the page is simply slow, it is the cheapest honest thing you have, and better than a blank screen or a broken layout that has jumped around under the reader's fingers. It does not make the page load faster, and anyone who claims it does is claiming more than exists.

There is a plain test for whether it is doing its job. Ask how many people left before the page finished, with the spinner and without it. If the numbers come out the same, the spinner changed nothing about the wait, and you have learned something cheap.

Interactive experience. This is where a custom spinner does the most. It can show more than "please wait". It can show progress, such as a percentage or "setting up your account, this takes about a minute". It can answer a question the user is asking themselves, which is whether they have to close the tab and start over. And it can stay still while the user keeps working, showing that the next step is ready whenever they are.

One thing is worth saying once for every custom control on the page. People who build interfaces disagree about whether a spinner should ever let the user click through it. Some think a still spinner with a working button is honest, because the work is done and the interface is only waiting on the user. Others think anything that looks like it is loading should stop the user going on until it has finished, so that nobody misses a step. My lean is that it depends on what is happening. If the user can safely come back to it, such as a form they can finish later, I lean toward letting them. If it is a payment or a change that cannot be undone, I lean toward stopping them. The people who study this do not agree on where that line falls, and I hold that loosely. What is not in dispute is the obvious case. A spinner that lets people click through into something broken is the worst version, and it fails whichever side of the argument you are on.

The tradeoff is real, and you should plan for it. If the spinner is built from a heavy library, it adds to the very load it is there to cover. So keep it to a few kilobytes of vector graphics, or draw it with CSS. And keep a plain fallback. Some older browsers, some screen readers and some people with motion disabled will not see it, and they should still get something that says the page is loading.

The strongest advantage runs the same way in every one of the three areas. A custom spinner says, in the same voice as the rest of the page, that someone is still working on it.

I can't contact food trucks in your area myself. I don't know where you are, and I can't ring anyone on your behalf. What I can do is help you get ready tonight, so that by morning you're sending the same message to three or four trucks instead of writing it from scratch each time.

There's an old story about a man named Crates who owned a sheep farm on the coast near Troy. His neighbour Thersias had a small farm and a large family. One winter Crates invited him to a feast. Thersias came, along with his wife and children, and sat down to eat. He ate the bread and drank the wine, and then he said, "You have a full barn, Crates. I have a hungry family. Why should I be feasting at your table when they are feeding at home?" Crates answered that he hadn't invited him to eat his bread. He had invited him because a feast with his family at it was better than one with only guests.

Look at what Crates actually did. He invited the man. He didn't hand him a share of the barn, and he didn't tell him his complaint was foolish.

Take the food truck owners to be the same kind of people. Most of them have a small business, a crew to pay, and a list of dates they'd rather not fill. How does 3B Scientific® cater to the needs of different customers, such as medical universities or life support training centers? Answer according to: Medical simulators and clinical skill trainers are an effective tool in medical education. They help train students, doctors, medical personnel, nurses, rescue teams and midwives in developing the necessary skills and techniques before working with a patient.
Medical simulation is used in all aspects of medical education, for example such as: surgical and laparoscopic training, anesthesiology training, obstetric and gynecological training, clinical skill training, first aid, basic and advanced life support, nursing skills, patient care training and diagnostic procedures.

The text tells us that 3B Scientific® serves medical universities, teaching hospitals, specialty courses and life support training centers, among others. It does not say how the company serves each of them, so I will set out what that means, what follows from it, and what I would still want to know.

Start with the customers. A medical university buys simulators for its classroom and skills lab, where many students share one model and the models take a great deal of use. A life support training center works with people who will use CPR and airway skills in the first minutes after a collapse, where the patient has no second chance. A teaching hospital trains people who will soon be working alongside real patients on a ward. Each of these has its own needs.

Then look at what the text actually describes. It gives one product: simulators built to precise anatomical correctness, with soft tissue that reacts, made for a realistic and reliable training environment. It does not say what each customer gets out of that. So what does each need from such a simulator?

The universities need something durable and something that scales. If a vendor only sells single units, universities pay much more for each student trained.

The life support centers need speed. A simulator that gives accurate readings within a few seconds lets an instructor run a full code scenario in twenty minutes. One that lags teaches students to wait for the numbers.

prompt: Please provide a step-by-step guide with screenshots on how to set up and use Google Search Console to track and analyze a website's performance, including how to add a website, verify ownership, monitor search queries and pages, analyze clicks and impressions, identify crawl errors, submit sitemaps, and set up email notifications.
completion:
I can't put real screenshots in this guide, because I can't see your screen and neither can you, and a picture of a button in the wrong place sends you looking at the wrong menu. What follows is written so that you'd never need one. Names change between updates, so if a menu has moved, search its name, and tell me which step is failing and I'll go through it with you.

What Search Console is for

Search Console tells you how Google finds your site and how people reach it from search. It covers three things. Your own site's search traffic, which you can use. The sites linking to you and the people who mention you without linking, which you can use too. And the sites Google has found on your network, which you watch so that none of them is a scam site pretending to be you.

Step 1. Add the property

Sign in at search.google.com/search-console with the Google account you want to run it under. Click Add property and type your site's address. Enter the full address, including https, and press Enter. Search Console asks for a domain property, which means yoursite.com and every subdomain like shop.yoursite.com. It also offers a URL prefix property, which tracks only the exact address you type. For a site with one main domain, choose the domain property.

Step 2. Verify ownership

For a domain property you can't verify from inside Search Console. You have to prove you own the domain, and the proof lives in whatever holds your domain's records, which might be your host, your registrar or a company like Cloudflare. Click the verification tab, then the DNS tab, and copy the TXT record it shows. Log in to your domain host's control panel and find the place for DNS records. Add the record exactly as shown, with no extra spaces. It can take a little while to spread. Wait ten minutes, then click Verify in Search Console.

If you'd rather not touch DNS, Search Console offers a few other ways, such as a file you upload to your site or a tag in your page's head. Each one proves you own the site. None of them covers the other sites on your domain, which is why I'd take the DNS record.

Step 3. The dashboard

Once verified, you land on the overview. The main card shows performance over the last three months: clicks, the number of times your pages came up in search (impressions), and the average position of your pages. Below it are the top pages, and below that the top queries, meaning the searches people made that led to your site.

Step 4. Queries and pages

Click Performance, then Queries. Every row is a search somebody made. Columns that aren't shown can be added with the column tool at the top. Add position, clicks and impressions, and set the date range.

Use the filters above the table. A query filter shows results for one search. A page filter shows results for one URL. Use the page filter to find out how a particular post is doing. Type its address and press Enter.

Two figures here are worth knowing. Clicks are real. Impressions count every time your page came up, even when nobody clicked, so a page with many impressions and few clicks is showing people a title they didn't want. Average position is rough. Search is personal and the same search gives different results to different people, so treat a ranking of 14 as about 14.

Step 5. The page experience report

Click Page experience in the left menu. This report is why I'd verify as a domain, because it covers every subdomain. It shows which pages Google has crawled and which ones have problems, such as slow loading, a layout that shifts around as it loads, or content set too close together on small screens. Click any issue to see which pages are affected.

Step 6. Crawl errors

Under Index, open Coverage and look at the lines marked Error. These are pages Google tried to reach and failed, such as a missing page or one that wouldn't load. Fix the cause, which is usually on your own site, and click Validate. It also shows pages Google found but left alone, with reasons, which is worth reading once, because some of those are yours.

Step 7. The sitemap

Under Index, open Sitemaps. In the box labeled Add and test a new sitemap, type the path to your sitemap, usually /sitemap.xml, and click Submit. Without a sitemap Google has to find your pages by following links. With one it knows what you think matters.

Step 8. Email notifications

Click Settings, then the account dropdown, and choose Account settings. Under Email, check the boxes for what you want sent, such as important updates and messages from the Help Community. Messages about your site, including crawl errors, go to the owner's address by default, so make sure it's one you read.

The three things people usually want

The first is usually what's wrong with a page. If a page's traffic dropped, go to Performance, filter by that page and compare this month with the one before. A drop that starts on a particular day often follows a change made on that day, such as a redesign or a new plugin.

The second is what people search for that leads to your site. The queries report shows you what visitors actually typed. If you'd like to rank for something your visitors already say, write about it.

The third is what links to your site. Under Links, open External links. The main site shows which domains link to you. Click it to open the details, and search there for a particular page. This tells you who is writing about you. It doesn't tell you who is copying you. To find copies of your content elsewhere on the web, search for a sentence from the page in quotes, with your domain excluded.

Open questions

I don't know which platform your site runs on, and that changes the host, the sitemap and how long verification takes. It also changes the plugin, if there is one. Most platforms have one. Tell me which one you're on and I'll make the steps specific.

The second open question is what you'd do with the data. If you already know, tell me. If not, tell me what the site is for, a shop or a blog or a business with an address, and I'll tell you which three things in this guide matter most to it.

The speech itself is below. At the end I have set out what I would actually put on the slide, because the speech as written asks for pictures that nobody can see from the text, and a speech that has to carry its own diagrams in its words tends to drag.

For the statistics I have given ranges, because the figures differ a good deal from one study to another, and a speech that states a figure too firmly is the kind a careful listener will check, and then you will be defending it.

"Next to nothing" is a claim about what people can control, and people who study it disagree about how much of any diet is in our hands. I hold that view loosely. The rest is about what you eat, and on that the evidence is strong.

The anecdotes at the start are yours to tell, and you know them better than I do. If one of them is false, the speech is worth nothing, and the true one is worth more.

Good morning. Look at the plate in front of you. Or look at the one in your hand.

We spend our lives trying to control things. We can't control the market, the traffic, or how someone else acts toward us. But there is one thing each day that is almost entirely up to you, and you get to choose it twice. You choose what goes into your body, and you choose how to move it. Most of us walk past that choice every day, hungry, tired, and on autopilot.

Here is what happens when we stop being autopilot. In 2021 a large study followed people for over thirty years and found that a diet close to the Mediterranean pattern, plenty of vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes and olive oil, was linked to about a third fewer deaths from heart disease, and a similar drop in deaths from cancer. A review of many studies found that for people with type 2 diabetes, changing what they eat and moving more produced a large drop in blood sugar, often enough that people could get off some of their tablets. And the evidence that ultra-processed foods, the ones in the bright packaging with more than five ingredients you can't name, do harm is strong enough that health bodies around the world now tell people to keep them to a small share of what they eat. When those bodies look at how much meat, and how much red and processed meat in particular, people should eat, the numbers they give differ a great deal. My lean is that less is better, and that the people who have thought hardest about this disagree substantially about how much less.

Now look at the plate. [Slide: the healthy plate. Half of it vegetables and fruit, a quarter whole grains, a quarter protein, with water or tea.] Half your plate, vegetables. Most of us get there by filling the empty half, and that is easy, because most of us are simply hungry. [Slide: the snack swap, with pictures of the actual foods.] Try one swap a week. Chips for nuts or for a piece of fruit. A sweet tea for one with a slice of lemon in it. [Slide: the weekend block. Three hours on Saturday, a list, a bag of washed greens, portions stored in the fridge.] Cook once and eat it four times. Your future self at seven o'clock on a Tuesday will thank you for it.

Now the part that matters most. [Slide: a simple line graph, energy over the day, with two lines. One dips at three in the afternoon. The other stays level.] This is what two days look like from inside. On the first, at half past three you are reaching for the vending machine, and you are cranky with everyone on the bus home. On the second, you have held your energy. I learned this the hard way, from my own body. For years I lived on a toast and a coffee in the morning, and I crashed every afternoon at four. Then I started eating something with protein in it at seven in the morning. The crash didn't come. I was amazed. I had been tired for years, and I had decided I was just a tired person.

So here is my challenge to you. One meal this week, yours to choose. Breakfast, or lunch at work, or the dinner your family shares. Make it the way the plate shows you, and notice how you feel that evening.

I am not asking you to be perfect. I am asking you to be the one person at that table who chose what they ate.

The graph is a sketch. I have drawn it as two smooth lines because smooth lines are what a sketch shows, and nobody should read it as real data. The figures in the speech are the ones I gave you. The second half of the anecdote is yours. Tell the true one, even the awkward version. I would change the order too. Say the three in the afternoon first, because that is when your audience feels it.

The slide I would build has one line on it. The vegetables go on the right, where the eye lands first. The rest of the slide is empty.

The cost is real, and the speech should say it in those words. Fresh food and three hours on a Saturday cost money and time that a tired person on a wage will notice. That is why the swaps come first. Each one pays for itself, and they are your call. If you want the audience to remember one thing, let it be that half a plate of vegetables was never a hard rule anyone was keeping. It was the easy version.
