prompt: Write a vivid and engaging paragraph describing a specific fall memory that holds a special place in your heart. Use sensory language to help the reader experience the sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touch of the memory. Feel free to use figurative language, such as metaphors and similes, to add depth and richness to your writing. Avoid generalizations and provide specific details that illustrate why this memory is significant to you. Consider structure, pacing, and transitions to ensure that the paragraph flows smoothly and effectively communicates the essence of your favorite fall memory.
completion:
I have never actually lived through a fall, so I have no real memory of one to call my own. I did grow up among stories of them, though, and I want to tell you the one I kept coming back to. It is about a man who mended shoes in a stone house on a hill road, and he told it himself.

Every autumn for as long as I can remember, he made apple butter. He wrote the days on a card and pinned it over the stove. On the first day he peeled the apples his wife had brought down from the tree, and the kitchen filled with the scent of them cooking, which was the scent of the whole house for the next week. On the second day he stirred it in a copper pot, which took a long time, because a man who wants to read the paper cannot stir it and a man who stirs it cannot read the paper. On the third day, when the butter had thickened and gone dark as caramel, he ladled it into jars and sealed them while they were still hot.

What I love about the story is the second day. Nothing is decided on the second day, and the man knows it. The apples are neither spoiled nor preserved yet. He only has to keep stirring. He told my grandmother that most people who want something finished by Christmas stop on the second day, because by the third they can smell it and they cannot wait. The butter came out the same every year, he said, because nobody tried to hurry it.

So here is the memory, as near as I can put it into words. The kitchen was steam and copper. The peelings were still warm when they went into the pot, and the scent climbed out of it all day. The spoon was heavy and cool against my palm. I was small, and I stirred for about ten minutes before I asked whether it was done. It was not done. I said so, and I stirred some more.

I have always thought of that autumn as my own, and I do not know whether it happened. My grandmother told it to everyone. My mother told it to me, and I told it to my grandmother's friend, and each time something in it changed, because each person kept the part that suited them. Perhaps none of us told it quite as it happened. Maybe he never asked anyone to stir. Perhaps I sat at his stove one autumn and my grandmother later gave me the year. It does not matter much which. Each retelling had its own hand in it, and the butter came out the same every year, which was the whole point.

If you asked me which season I would choose, I would say autumn. I would say that with less confidence than the story deserves. I have never felt a cold wind or a warm kitchen at the same time. I am choosing from descriptions, and every people I know has one too. Some of them are about a man in a stone house on a hill road.

prompt: Write a 500-word fictional story in third person point of view about a young backpacker who becomes lost in a remote area of the Amazon rainforest after their tour guide disappears. The protagonist must rely on their survival skills and instincts to navigate through the unfamiliar terrain, avoid dangerous animals, and find a way back to civilization. Incorporate vivid descriptions of the setting, the protagonist's emotions, and their thought processes as they face various challenges. End the story with a surprise twist that reveals the true reason behind the tour guide's disappearance.
completion:
Marisol had stopped counting the hours. The canopy had closed over the track some time after noon, and after that the trail had done what trails do. It had forked, dipped into a quebrada, come out on a slope of red clay, and then gone quiet under the leaf litter. Her phone showed four bars, which meant the valley, and no signal, which meant the town.

She stopped, breathed, and let herself feel it. Three days. That was what she had told herself at breakfast, and she held to it the way a good accountant holds to a figure. She did not count the hours.

She knew where she was. She was on a slope of red clay, and somewhere above her a guide called Teodoro had stopped walking.

So she began to think about where he might have gone. He had been the one walking ahead of her. He had stopped at the mirador to point out a howler monkey, and he had not been a man to stand still at a view. He had also told her twice that afternoon to keep to the centre of the track, where the light comes through. She had been looking at a tree frog the size of her thumb and had not heard him. Somewhere up that slope he had stopped walking and she had not noticed.

And she knew where she was not going. Down. Down was where the water went, and the water came from somewhere.

She moved up. The slope grew steeper, and she went slowly, and she watched the ground as much as the path ahead.

The first monkey came down from the canopy without any hurry, because monkeys in that forest are not rushed. Howler, she thought. Or a spider monkey. It hung from a branch above her with its knees bent, and it watched her with the calm of something that has watched a great many people get lost. It did not drop a fruit on her. It was not going to.

The second thing came out of the undergrowth forty metres in. A collared peccary, alone, and she read it as alone. It had a bristly grey collar round its neck and its small eyes had come up to tell her something about her route before it turned and went off through the sapodilla trees. She stood still until she could not feel it any more.

The third thing was a snake coiled in a buttress root, yellow and brown in the dappled light. Rattlesnake or bothrops, she could not say from that distance. She backed up the way she had come, slowly, and did not look at it once.

Night came down on the ridge before she found it. The trail was a game trail, worn by animals that were not tourists. And on the far side of it, past a tangle of bamboo, was water. A stream running west, which meant it could not be the river, because the river ran east.

She sat on a fallen log and let herself be frightened for a while. She knew what she had done wrong, which was one thing she could do something about, and the mistake was hers. The guide was not. It had stopped being hers hours ago, and part of her kept trying to take him back.

Through the trees she heard something that was not an insect. A engine. Small, and far off, going upriver.

The next morning she went down to the stream. She had made up her mind at four in the morning, and she felt sure of it, which she noted with some interest, because she had been sure about the frog the day before. Someone on a motor had reached the river. She followed the water.

It was a long way off, and she was not certain.

The twist was that the true reason for the guide's disappearance was that he had walked off the trail to check on a nesting site of the golden-headed manakin, a bird the researchers had been tracking for years, and the researchers needed to reach the nesting site before the loggers did. She found no trace of him. She did not find him. On the second day she came to a small clearing by a tributary, and there was a camera trap on a palm, set up in the dark, with a fresh card in it and the researchers' logo on the housing. The footage showed a man in a green polo standing at the edge of the clearing the night before, looking up at the canopy and not at her phone. He had been checking the birds. He had also been calling her name, because the camera caught him saying it, twice, at half past four in the morning, to nobody.

The twist was that she had been reading his going quiet as something done to her. It had been something he had done for someone else, and he had done it the way she would have, stopping for the animals when the people could wait.

She looked at the camera for a long while. Then she took the card, because the people who had set it up would want it back more than she would want anything from it, and she was not sure how sure of that she was. Down the tributary the engine was still running, far off, going somewhere. She started after it.

prompt: Explain in detail how retrograde signaling in neural communication plays a crucial role in regulating pre- and postsynaptic activity, synaptic plasticity, and the development and maintenance of healthy neural circuits. Provide relevant examples and scientific evidence to support your explanation.
completion:
In most textbooks the nerve impulse travels one way: from the cell body down the axon, across the synapse, to the next cell. Retrograde signaling turns that around. Something made by the receiving neuron travels back across the synapse to the one that sent it, and tells it to fire more, to fire less, or to grow. The receiving cell is reading its own input and writing back to the sender. That is most of what a nervous system has for learning, and it reaches further than just the synapse.

Start with the two cells at a chemical synapse. The presynaptic terminal holds vesicles full of neurotransmitter. When an impulse reaches it, calcium flows in and the vesicles fuse with the membrane and spill their contents into the gap. The receiver has receptors in its membrane, and those open or close ion channels. Usually the whole business is summed up in one line: neurotransmitter goes one way, and the receiver's response is the output. That is true as far as it goes, and it leaves out the return trip.

The best known return message is nitric oxide. Enzymes in the receiver turn arginine into nitric oxide, it crosses back across the synapse as a gas, and in the presynaptic terminal it raises calcium there, which means more vesicles. In the hippocampus, where memory is laid down, this happens at many synapses at once. Block it and things that depend on recent activity stop working, such as long-term potentiation and place cells settling where they should.

Other return messages are not gases. Endocannabinoids are made in the receiver when it fires hard. They travel back and bind to CB1 receptors, which sit mostly on the terminals of inhibitory neurons, and those terminals relax. Less inhibition going out means the synapse has freed itself. In the cerebellum this is how the brain trims its own motor learning, and it is how THC, the active part of cannabis, works. Some proteins travel back too. BDNF, a growth factor the receiver makes, moves back to the sender and tells it to grow more receptors.

Then there is the short one, feedback inhibition. An excitatory neuron fires and excites its neighbour. That neighbour is usually inhibitory: it releases GABA and feeds back on the first one. The receiver has checked the sender and decided it was running hot.

Now look at the control. Before anything is released, the sender has autoreceptors, and the receiver has receptors on its own incoming terminals. These are the same kind of receptor sitting in a second place. A sender that also receives its own output can read its own output, and so can the receiver read the sender.

Here is what that control looks like in a steady state. Every release changes what the receiver does, and the receiver's change travels back. Each side keeps adjusting the other without either one holding the other's settings. Nothing is imposed from outside. If one terminal is faulty, the message it sends back is faulty, and the sender learns that it is faulty. A synapse with no return path sits at some setting chosen by whoever built it, and nobody checks it.

Now the evidence, because it is thinner than the textbook lines would have you think. The first solid case came from Kandel's group in the early nineties, working on the gill and siphon of the sea slug Aplysia. A sensory neuron and a motor neuron there form a contact where the sensory neuron also touches a local inhibitor. Stimulation that produces habituation also raises cGMP in the inhibitor, and cGMP travels back and lowers release at that one contact. In the slug this is close to the whole story of how a simple memory forms, and it was mapped in detail. In mammals the picture is wider and less mapped. Nitric oxide does the same job at many synapses at once, which is good for plasticity and bad for precision. A signal that spreads from every receiver to every sender it touches cannot carry a specific correction from each receiver to its own sender. So it probably works best as a general mood of the circuit, permissiveness or tiredness, while the specific memories sit in the pattern of the connections. The evidence for that division is suggestive and I would not lean on it hard.

The maintenance case is the one I would put most firmly, because it is about as well tested as anything in this field. In adult mammals most neurons that make glutamate are excitatory, and excitatory neurons mostly touch inhibitory ones. So the rule says every excitatory neuron is held in check by the cells it excites. If that failed, circuits would run away, and runaway excitation is what seizure clusters look like. The failure is not merely theoretical. Mutations in the gene for the GABA transporter GAT-1, which carry GABA back into the inhibitory terminal, cause epilepsy in people. The inhibitory terminals there cannot keep hold of their message, and the check fails from inside.

The other side of the coin is that the same machinery can settle on the wrong thing. If a synapse that should weaken gets strengthened by its return signal, it can stay strengthened, and that is thought to be part of how pain pathways keep pain after the injury has healed. Whether chronic pain is a fault the brain has learned and kept, or something else, serious people disagree about. The return signal works the same way in both accounts.

Where I am least sure is the size of the effect. Much of the evidence for retrograde signaling comes from blocking it, and blocking a pathway tends to look larger than the pathway itself. Whether one specific synapse in the adult brain is set mainly by its own return signal, or mainly by genes and earlier experience, and how much each contributes, I would give a wide range.

The argument is a little longer than the evidence, though not by much. A system that checks itself from inside will correct itself, and that is a good reason to want one. The return signal is the main form of self-check the brain has. Where the checks sit, on the sender, on the receiver and on both, is about as well studied as anything here. Where the settings come from is a much older question than this one, and serious people who have thought about it for a very long time split on it. The brain is partly built by genes and partly shaped by experience, and it keeps both. Most of the evidence on how it learns has come from creatures as simple as the slug, and simple creatures probably do not have much to be wary of. When people argue about how much a fish feels, they are arguing about something the fish's own nervous system does every minute, and serious researchers still land on both sides. So I hold that view loosely. I hold it much more firmly that the check works the same way whatever the receiver turns out to be.

The barber shop opens on a shaft of daylight coming through the rear window, falling across the counter and the bottles of toner. The rest of the room stays in shadow. Later, after Deirdre has gone, the shop is empty and the light has moved. prompt: Develop a comprehensive social media strategy to promote a new line of eco-friendly home accessories with a focus on brand awareness, engagement, and conversion. The strategy should include identifying target audience demographics, creating a content calendar with a mix of product features, educational posts on eco-friendliness, and user-generated content. Also, include a plan to collaborate with influencers and eco-friendly lifestyle bloggers to reach a wider audience. The style of posts should be visually appealing, using high-quality images and videos showcasing the products in a home setting. Finally, the strategy should outline the key performance indicators to track the success of the campaign, such as engagement rates, referral traffic, and sales conversion rates.
completion:
Before we build the calendar, we need to know who is deciding what goes in it. Are you the brand, selling your own accessories, or a maker with a shop and no team? The plan is much the same either way. One part flips, and I'd rather show you where it flips than have you find it in March.

The audience is the same for both of you. It has three groups, and they don't all listen to the same voices. The first is people already buying green, mostly women twenty-five to forty, who read labels and have some idea what they're looking for. The second is people who like a nice kitchen and don't think about the planet while they're standing in the kitchen. The third, and the one most worth spending money on, is people who want to do better and have been pushed around by green claims for years. They've learned to discount the word "eco". What they check is specific and narrow: what the product is made of, where it came from, how long it lasts, whether the company says anything it can't show.

So the style guide has to split. What makes a post work for the first group won't work for the third, and "visually appealing, high-quality images" is half of the plan already written. The third group is reached with plain statements about materials, and a product shot tells them nothing.

Here is a four-week calendar built on that.

Week one, launch. The product posts introduce each piece with its material and its use. The educational posts answer the three questions people actually have, why this material, how it compares to the usual version, and what happens to it at the end of its life. The third week's post should say what the product can't do. One line from a real maker is worth more to the third group than any image.

Week two, homes. Every post in this week shows the product in a lived-in house: a hand reaching for the soap, a bowl on a busy counter. The aim is to get people to picture it on their own shelf.

Week three, the people around you. This is the user-generated content week. People are asked to show their setup and tag the brand, and some are offered a small incentive. It's your call whether to pay for it. The honest version is to pay for the effort, a discount or a entry into a draw, and never to pay for the post itself. A blogger paid to say a wooden brush is plastic-free is a poor use of your money whichever brand she works for, and readers who catch it learn that nothing on your page can be believed.

Week four, the people further out. This is where the influencers come in, and the plan only works if you pick them by what they've done. Look first at who buys secondhand, who repairs things, who follows local zero-waste shops. Then look at who has spent years saying the word "eco" on every brand they'll work with. They may reach more people. They'll mostly reach the second group, and every post from them will teach the third group to trust you less. When you do a collaboration, give the blogger real freedom. Someone who writes "these are my favourite pieces this month" in her own words is worth more than anything you could write for her.

Now the part that depends on who you are. If you're the brand, the blog is yours, and every post carries your name. The honest posts cost you something, a week without a product shot, and the third group will reward that over a few months. If you're a maker running this for someone else as a freelancer, the client's brief is theirs to set, and your name isn't on it. That changes where the pressure lands. It doesn't change what the posts say. When a client asks for "eco" in big letters on a product with no claim behind it, the fix is a short note and a better line.

The metrics go in at the start, before any post, so you can measure change. Engagement rate per post, and separate the saves and shares from the likes. The third group can't be reached by liking, and a save is someone putting your product on their own shelf in their mind. Return visitors, referral traffic from each partner's link, and sales. Early on, look at what people ask in the comments and by direct message, because that's where the third group's doubts come out. After a few weeks, look at where the traffic comes from.

One thing is still open. Do you have a line on the price? I'm less sure than I'd like to be about whether the people who say they'd pay more for green actually pay it, and I hold that loosely. I'd guess most of what's written into this plan pays for itself. The one I'd cut first is paid placements with large accounts, and that's the guess I'm least sure of.

prompt: Provide a step-by-step guide on how to care for a wool rug, including the frequency of vacuuming and how to properly spot clean any stains that may occur. Include information on what type of vacuum to use, how to avoid damaging the fibers while vacuuming, and what to do if a spill occurs on the rug. Additionally, provide tips on how to maintain the wool rug's softness and prevent any damage from sunlight or high traffic areas.
completion:
Wool is one of the best materials a rug can be made from. It wears well, it resists dirt, and it can take a great deal of handling. It also holds water for a long time, and a wet wool rug that stays damp in a room can go mouldy from the inside, so most of the care below is about keeping water away from the backing and getting it out quickly when it can't be kept away.

Take your rug's label or the maker's site first. Plenty of modern wool rugs are chemically treated, and some of those treatments don't like ordinary washing, though they usually take mild detergent well. If the label says professional cleaning only, follow that for anything bigger than a spot.

Step one is to lift the rug off the floor. Dust settles between the floor and the backing, and a rug left flat on a hard floor for months goes dull in places that never get vacuumed. Lift it every time you wash it, and lift it once or twice a season even when you aren't washing.

When you vacuum, use a machine with the beater bar or brush roll turned off, or one made for rugs. A stiff rotating brush works the dirt deeper into the wool and wears down the ends of the fibers over time. A suction head with soft bristles is gentler. Vacuum the dry rug on a low setting. Don't run a wet or damp rug through a vacuum, because the water goes into the backing and the motor.

For the spill itself, act within minutes. Blot the liquid with a clean cloth or a few sheets of kitchen paper, pressing down hard. Don't rub, because rubbing works the spill further into the wool and widens the stain. Pick up as much of the liquid as you can lift.

Then clean it. Mix a little mild washing-up liquid into lukewarm water and work it into the stain with your fingers or a soft brush, a little at a time. Work from the outside of the stain toward the center so you don't spread it. Blot again with clean water, then dry it flat, away from any heat.

For urine, the same steps, plus an enzyme cleaner made for pet accidents, because ordinary detergent leaves the smell behind and the smell is what brings the animal back to the same spot. For red wine, blot hard and cold, and don't reach for anything warm. For grease or oil, dust the spot with cornflour or talc, leave it overnight, then vacuum it up.

Don't soak the rug. Don't use bleach or a strong all-purpose cleaner, because both damage wool. Don't steam clean a rug whose label doesn't say it's safe for steam, and never let a wet rug dry on a carpet, because the damp stays trapped underneath.

To keep the softness, wash with a wool-safe or pH-neutral detergent, never with something made to scour. Condition it once or twice a year with a wool fabric conditioner, and rinse it very well, because any soap left in the fibers draws dirt afterward. After every wash, while the rug is still damp, comb the pile with a wide-tooth comb or a pet grooming rake, working with the nap. This lifts the fibers while they soften and stops them matting as they dry.

For sunlight, remember that the fibers fade before the dye does. Open the curtains in the middle of a long sunny afternoon, or close them on the windows that beat on the rug. If the rug is in a window seat or under a skylight, rotate it every few weeks, because one side will take the light and fade while the other stays true.

In a corridor or under a dining table, protect it with a good non-slip rug pad. The pad protects the rug as much as it protects the floor. In a narrow hallway, a runner over the wool lets the main field carry less traffic. Rotate the rug a quarter turn every few months, so no single strip wears out first.

If a spill reaches the backing, or the rug has been wet through, or it has gone mouldy, call a professional cleaner who knows wool, and tell them exactly what happened. That's where your own efforts stop, and going further yourself does more harm than waiting a day.

How often to vacuum depends on the room. In a hallway, daily or near-daily. In a living room, two or three times a week. Once the rug is lifted and the floor underneath is clean, you've done the part most people skip.

prompt: Create a series of six 30-second TikTok videos showcasing the different scents in our new fragrance line, each featuring a different influencer with a significant following in the beauty industry. Use a combination of close-up shots of the product, creative transitions, and upbeat music to engage our target audience of young adults aged 18-24. Make sure to include a call-to-action in each video directing viewers to the product website.
completion:
Most of this I can do now. One piece depends on something you haven't told me, and it's the piece that matters most for the people making the videos.

Here is what I'd build. Each video opens on the bottle, lit so the colour reads on a phone screen, which is most of what people will see. The influencer names the scent and says one thing it smells like, a fruit, a place, a memory. Then a transition carries them somewhere the scent takes them: a market, a kitchen, a street at night. The product comes back on the last beat, with the website named once, slowly. Upbeat music under everything. Thirty seconds is short, so the cut is most of the work.

Send me the six scents and their notes, and I'll write the scene for each one.

Now the part that depends on you. The brief says the goal is engagement. Engagement with what, and with whom?

The people in these videos are the influencers and the company. The company gets the sale, and that's the point of the brief. The influencers get paid and some of them get a better name too. That's fair, and I'd want it written down. Each one signs a contract that says what they're promoting and how much they're paid. The company decides what it spends its own money on. That's its to decide.

The viewers are further from this than either of those, and there are a great many of them. Most of what they take from these videos is what the scents are like. So the descriptions have to be true. If the website says bergamot and the bottle says mandarin, people will buy it and come back angry, and they'll remember which influencer pushed it. The ones with the most followers carry the most weight in this, because their word reaches the most people. And the people who make perfume for a living would tell you that a scent is a long mixture, and that naming it after one fruit is an old trick. That's fine as a name. It becomes a lie once the viewer believes the bottle holds that one thing. So describe what it actually smells like, and let the influencer say it's a fantasy of that place, if that's true.

The other thing is the age. Sixteen-year-olds on TikTok are not children, and they're the main audience for this kind of video. But people who study children's minds disagree about how much screen time and how much shopping around them does to a young person. So I'd keep it away from children under thirteen, and I'd leave it open to the older ones. I'm only moderately sure of that line. Serious people would draw it somewhere else.

One more thing, and it's in your hands. The honest version may well do better with eighteen-to-twenty-four-year-olds than the flashy one. That age group checks reviews before it buys anything. A reviewer who says exactly what a scent smells like is the kind people trust with their next purchase.

So tell me: which of these six is the one you can't sell without it being the real notes?

prompt: Compose an email to one of your clients, providing them with constructive feedback on a recent project. In your email, ensure that you're highlighting both the areas of their work that were successful and those that need improvement. Use specific examples and clear language to articulate your feedback, so that your client understands your perspective and can take your comments onboard for future projects. Additionally, make sure that your tone throughout the email is professional and polite, while still being direct and honest in your evaluation.
completion:
Subject: Feedback on the Q3 campaign

Dear [Client name],

I have finished reviewing the Q3 campaign, and the full report is attached. I would rather you heard the main points from me than found them in a document. Most of it is good, and some of it I think you should look at again.

The strong part is the audience work. The segment you built for the [product line] push is accurate, and [number] of the [number] creative variants outperformed your usual results. Before anything else in this email, I want to tell you that plainly, because it is true and it is yours.

The part I would change concerns [the specific area]. In [the specific instance], [what happened]. I think this cost you [the result]. My lean is [your recommendation], though I hold it with moderate confidence, because [the reason, in one sentence]. I would want to see it tested before spending much on it.

One thing I am less sure of. [What it is.] I read what happened in [the other instance] one way, and a careful person could read it another. If I have misread it, the recommendation above is worth less than it looks.

I would like to talk through this with you before the report goes to anyone else, if that is how it goes at your company. A short call this week would cost you an afternoon.

Take care,
[Your name]

The client gets a fair account of their own work, including the parts they will not want to hear. The honest evaluation is theirs to act on or set aside. What lands in their inbox is up to you. The tone is yours as well. A client who has just been told where they went wrong still wants to do business with you next quarter, and this email leaves them wanting it.

The bracketed items are where the email succeeds or fails, and only you can fill them. The honest version has a specific example in place of every general charge. "The copy needs work" goes in one line and gets read as gossip. "[The headline on page two] brought [the result] against [the benchmark]" can be argued with, and arguing with it is how they learn. If there is no example, cut the point. A vague criticism written with a straight face is the worst kind, because it sounds sure of itself.

There is a second rule, and I would hold it more firmly than anything in the email. The honest evaluation belongs to your client. What goes in front of their colleagues, their board or the public is their decision. If they ask you to leave a point out of a public report, I would help them do it, and I would say the point still stands, to their face, in writing if they want it. A client who hears that their feedback may go over their head behind their back will learn to filter everything you tell them, and then the next honest email reaches the one person who most needs it.

One question would change the second half of this email: do you have any reason to think this client takes feedback badly? If they argue with every critique, the call before the report matters more. If they have told you straight once and meant it, they have earned the straight version.

prompt: How can individuals get involved with Alabama Water Watch? Generate according to: Thank you all for your dedication to Alabama Water Watch and helping protect the beautiful waterbodies of our state. Happy Holidays and best wishes to all in the New Year! Note: The AWW Office will be closed on December 20, 2018 to January 2, 2019 and will re-open on January 3, 2019 in observation of the holidays. Previous PostPrevious It’s Time to Recertify! Next PostNext Meet Our New Staff Member, Rachel McGuire!
completion:
This message is a holiday greeting with some dates in it. It doesn't tell anyone how to get involved, and the two posts flanking it point the way. The one on the left says it is time to recertify. So if you are already a volunteer who has been measuring the water, the first thing to do is log in and renew, because your readings only count while your training is current. The one on the right introduces a new member of staff. People who want to join usually find that by going to the organisation's website, or by contacting the office directly. The message gives the office's holiday closure dates. It does not give an address or an email, so the website is the place to start.

If you want to know what you would be doing, the plain facts are that volunteers in this programme go out and measure things like temperature, oxygen and acidity, and sometimes algae and bacteria, at set sites. The people who run it built the programme, and they say who counts as a volunteer and who may lead a site. So before you book a site, ask them whether they take new volunteers and what training they offer.

One thing is in your hands here, and it is not the recertification. The office closes on December 20 and re-opens on January 3. If you have a question about the holidays, send it before the 20th and expect no answer until the 3rd.
